maintopic: SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

speechtext:
Hon. Mr. MEIGHEN moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 95, to assist returned soldiers in settling upon the land. He said:
This proposed legislation, as its name implies, is designed to assist returned soldiers in becoming settlers on land in Canada. In 1917 the Dominion Parliament passed the Soldiers' Settlement Act of that year which had the same general object in view, but the scope of whose operations was confined to lands owned by the Dominion. That is to say, the Bill did not make provision for the assistance of land settlement by soldiers, save to the extent that it provided an additional quarter-section for

each soldier, as a soldier's grant over and above his homestead rights, and to the -further extent that it enabled assistance to "be given to soldiers owning land by way *of a loan upon those lands on the ordinary loan basis. The main purpose of the present legislation, in so far as it is additional to and beyond the Bill of 1917, is to provide a means of acquiring lands now held privately or by corporations, or indeed by governments, for the purpose of disposing of those lands to returned soldiers. A foundation for the work we are now doing under the Soldiers' Settlement Board was first laid on the 11th February last by an Order in Council which in its provisions is similar to the corresponding provisions of the Bill now introduced. However, beyond the powers which, were taken by *the Order in Council referred to, this Bill provides a system and machinery whereby lands may be acquired other than by agreement or purchase, viz:	compulsorily and by expropriation. These ex-propriatory clauses contain means whereby, under a settlement area scheme, the lands that are being retarded from cultivation are set aside as settlement areas, and are thereby made subject to the compulsory provisions of the Bill. I have gone far enough to show that the measure i$ most comprehensive, and indeed progressive, in its character. It is, I think, the most extended and progressive federal land settlement scheme that has yet been brought to my attention. It is a Bill of considerable length and will demand much of the attention of Parliament.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	.

On the Orders of the Day:
Is the Government in a position to state definitely to the House when the report of the 'Civil Service Commission on the subject on the re-classification of the service will be laid upon the Table?

I am glad the
hon. gentleman has asked the question, as I intended to make a very brief statement upon the matter, il received this morning a telegram from the Secretary of the Postal Letter Carriers' Association, Mr. A. Mc-Mordie, of Toronto. I shall read that telegram and my reply thereto, which I think is quite comprehensive and fully covers the ground.
I might say that rumours have lately appeared in the press to the effect that a promise was given that the re-classification would be laid upon the table of the House, or introduced into Parliament, about the first of May. That is probably true; I think I made a statement myself to that effect. When I made that statement I was firmly of the opinion that the work of the Civil Service Commission would have been so far advanced that the classification report would be in the hands of Parliament by this time. However, that work up to the present moment was not fully completed, and it was therefore an utter impossibility for the Government to present the classification report to Parliament. Other statements have appeared in the press during the week to the effect that the classification would not be presented to Parliament during the present session of Parliament, but that it would be taken up at an adjourned session in the coming autumn, or at another session. This rumour, of course, is not correct; it is proposed that the classification shall be proceeded with during the present session. The telegram from Mr. McMordie to which I referred a moment ago reads as follows:
Much dissatisfaction amongst letter carriers, that the expectations of the Government as to Civil Service Commission report not materializing during the first week in May as promised. It is important that you give us definite statement now as to when this report will he submitted to the House of Commons.
To which I replied on May 12, as follows :

Your telegram eleventh received to-day. The work of classification by the Civil Service Commission is proceeding as rapidly as is humanly possible and nothing is being neglected to expedite this work. Classification work has taken a long time but it involved a stupendous task. The actual work is how about completed and a substantial proportion of schedules is printed. The printing is in two languages which involves also a translation but I think the printing will be wholly completed within fourteen days. On completion of printing a Bill to enact the classification will promptly be introduced into Parliament and advanced with all possible speed. I beg to assure your association that the work has been carried out with great earnestness since August last and it was not possible by any means to have had the work further advanced than it is although I was hopeful of its completion before this but I am satisfied no one is to blame for any delay. I hope your association will realize the Importance and comprehensiveness of the task and await the completion of the work which is now so nearly in sight.
I would like to say further, Mr. Speaker, that at the present moment the schedules are completed in the sense that all the preliminary work is done, and all that remains to be done prior to the introduction of the measure which will enact the classification, is the translation of the schedules and the printing. As a matter of fact, a very substantial proportion of the English translation is in print now, and also a very substantial proportion of the French translation is completed; and I am hopeful, as I have already stated, that within two weeks from to-day I shall be able to introduce a Bill providing for some amendments to the Civil Service Act and for the validation of the schedules.
Now, I wish to point out to the House- because this is a subject oF recent comment in the press and in some sections of the Civil Service-that the classification of the Inside and Outside Services is in all respects a stupendous task. It is the most comprehensive work of its character ever attempted by any country, and when it is finished it may well be regarded as the greatest accomplishment in 'this direction 'by any country.
The personnel of our Civil Service amounts to at least 50,000, and that is without taking into consideration the army and navy, our railway employees, the judiciary and some other branches of the public service. The classification work involved the making of 1,600 schedules, in the printing each page will take on the average about two and one half schedules, and when wholly printed it will mean a publication of six or seven hundred pages, which is quite a substantial volume. I wish also
to point out that a limited staff only could be employed in this work. I think it will be quite obvious that this work could not have been assigned to an unlimited number of men without substantial variations in principle being incorporated in the work, which would be very undesirable in settling the classification.
By way of comparison I might point out that some time ago the city of New York . made a classification of its Civil Service. The number of its employees was 60,000, slightly more than that of the Government of Canada, but I would imagine the work would be less complicated than our own. It took four years to complete that work, and it cost the city a great deal of money. As a further comparison I might mention the fact that a short time ago the state of New York made a classification of its Civil Service, which comprises 17,000 persons, and that took over two years. The Civil Service Commission of Canada have been employed since the first of August last in carrying out the directions given by Parliament in the Civil Service Act of last year, and I am sure every possible effort has been made and is being made to complete the work at an early date, and present it to Parliament for its consideration and, I hope, approval. With some slight knowledge of the vast deal of work which the commission has had to perform in connection with the classification I can confidently say that no complaint can fairly be made by the public or by any section of the Civil Service in regard to the time taken by the commission. However, as I stated a moment ago, I do expect that within two weeks I shall be able to present the report upon the classification of the Civil Service to Parliament and ask for approval of the same.
Before I sit down let me further point this out: When the classification with the schedules of salaries is approved by Parliament it will relate back to the beginning of the fiscal year; and if it happens that any members of the service are entitled under that classification to promotion in rank or in salary, the same will date back to the 1st of April last, and in that way no substantial wrong can be done to the personnel of- the Civil Service in the monetary sense by reason of an unexpected delay of a few weeks in the completion of the work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I move that subsection 3 of section 2 be amended by rescinding the words "in the holders thereof'' in lines 21 and 22, and substituting therefor the following: "in the Crown in the right of the Province of British Columbia." In justice to the Committee I think the clause might be explained. As every one knows, the Privy Council decided many years ago that the royal minerals, that is gold and silver, belonged to the province of British Columbia, while the baser metals belonged to the Dominion. An arrangement was arrived at by Order in Council for the working of the baser metals by means of sale to the province of those metals. The Order in Council of 1890-for Orders in Council are as old as that-provided that the baser metals might be sold, and that any one entering, in accordance with the law of the province for mining rights in the railway belt, would have a right to a lease of sufficient of the surface to enable

his mine to be worked. Then, when the forest reserves and parks were established, the difficulty immediately arose that if surface rights were alienated there, it would mean a very considerable interference with the use of the forest reserves and parks. Consequently it was provided that in the case of forest reserves and parks only a lease should be given subject to terms and conditions set down. This Bill provides for the continuance of that system, but provides also th'at wherever men acquired rights from the province of British Columbia prior to the establishment of the forest reserves and parks, then they might get a sale, because they would, under the previous law, be entitled to that sale of the surface rights and of the subsoil rights. Certain cases arose and were dealt with by Order in Council referred to in subsection 3, where men entered for mining rights prior to the establishment of forest reserves and rat a time when they were entitled to the subsoil and surface rights by sale. This amendment enables us to do the same in future wherever men acquired their rights prior to the establishment of reserves, and ratifies the action taken in the three individual cases.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What minerals are now vested in the right of the province, and what minerals are vested in the right of the Dominion? It might make the matter a little clearer if we knew what we were dealing with by these Orders in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The precious metals are the property of the province, and the baser meals belong to the Dominion. I cannot name in detail the precious metals, but undoubtedly they comprise gold, silver and copper. The main mineral that is ours is the coal, with which this Bill has to do chiefly. I am not certain as to iron, but I am of opinion that iron is a baser metal.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why was Order in Council No. 2156 passed vesting the mineral rights in the owners of the I. O. U., the 0. K. and the Apex Mineral Claims, and what were the conditions of that vesting?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The owners of those claims, had it not been for the establishment of the forest reserves, would have been entitled under the legislation of 1890 to surface rights granted by Order in Council. But after the forest reserves were established the Justice Department decided that the legislation of 1890 applied only to lands that were held by the Crown in the right of Canada, and not the lands reserved for sale. These lands were held for sale at the time the rights were acquired,-the

time the entries were made in accordance with the legislation of British Columbia,- and consequently it was only right that men who had acquired such rights should not be dispossessed of them by the subsequent establishment of forest reserves. The legislation does not apply to any one acquiring rights after that. Circumstances arose that made it necessary to take action. I do not remember the exact circumstances, but I think there was an issue of bonds or something of that nature. The hon. member for Caribou (Mr. Fulton) could tell more definitely about that than I. It was necessary that the rights of these people to which they were entitled at the time of acquirement, should be confirmed, and this legislation confirms the action taken.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why is it necessary to have that Order in Council ratified by Act of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not think it is legally necessary at all, but it is good constitutional practice to come to Parliament and say what was necessary to be done and have Parliament confirm it.

speechtext: Order in Council No. 2156 must have been passed under some provision of the law authorizing the Governor in Council to pass it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That being so, I fail to see
why it should be necessary to ratify it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Order in Council appointing the receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific was passed under statutory legislation. The Governor in Council had authority to pass it; nevertheless-

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is a question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
-as soon as it was
passed it came back to Parliament for ratification as a matter of constitutional practice. This Order in Council is in exactly the same position. ' It is not a legal necessity at all. Any continuing effect of the Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act has practically in law to cease upon the termination of the Act, which is upon the termination of the war. In order that its continuing effect may exist, it should be ratified by legislation. But in this case, as the effect is not in the nature of a continuing effect but rather something done, I do not think there is any legal necessity. It however is well to do it as a matter of constitutional practice.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If I understand the minister, that Order in Council, No. 2156, was passed in virtue of the War Measures Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am not quite certain
of the Act. It is usual to name as many Acts as you can when you pass an Order in Council. It is very probable that it was passed under the Dominion Lands Act or the War Measures Act and any other which would be opportune. That is good practice that I commend to my hon. friend when he becomes a member of a Government.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think that is an eventuality that may never materialize, but before That time comes I would like to go into this matter a little farther. If, for the enactment of this Order in Council a basis had to be found in the provisions of the War Measures Aot, I think this House should go more carefully into it and ascertain what is the opinion of the Minister of Justice as to the right of the owners of these mineral claims. I would like, before we pass this clause, that the opinion of the Minister of Justice on the rights of these owners be laid on the table of the House so that we may examine the matter more carefully.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There has been no *
written opinion given, but I have no hesitation in giving the opinion, which will now go on Hansard, that their rights are quite secure.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The opinion of the Acting
Minister of Justice that the rights of the owners of these claims are quite secure is not an answer to my question. 1 am now asking whether these claimants had really a right to receive from the Crown the grant of the title to these mineral claims. The minister said that they had some vested rights, and that it was only just and fair that the Crown should remit those vested rights in the surface and the minerals in the claims. It not having been provided by law that the 'Government should have such a Tight, the minister tells us now that it had probably been found necessary-without being absolutely sure of the point-to revert to tlhe War Measures Act to find authority to pass an Order in Council with reference to the rights of tbe owners of these claims. I believe we should very carefully go into the question and ascertain what their rights are. The minister said that they had a right 4 p.m. to these claims but I would like to see what their title is. I would like to know if they had a clear title to these claims and in what way their title takes priority to the title of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I thought I explained that. These people entered their claims prior to the establishment of the reserve.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Prior to the establishment of the reserve. That is the only point of any importance. When the law of 1890 applied, it gave to the entrant of these claims, who complied with the British Columbia regulations, the right to the acquirement of the surface to the extent necessary to work the claims. That right was intact. But it had not been granted as they had not made proof and we knew nothing about it. Subsequently this Parliament establishes a reserve; that statute takes away the right, in the opinion of the Justice Department, because the law of 1890 did not apply to land unless it was held for sale. These claimants find themselves in that position when they come to apply. I do not think anything could be clearer than that it is our duty to put them in the position they were in prior to the establishment of the reserve. Is that clear to the hon. gentleman?

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Was there any provision in the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act to give to the Government authority so to do?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, that is why this legislation is necessary. It was not known at the time that there were any rights there. It only becomes known afterwards when these people apply and say that they come under the British Columbia law.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I think the point made by my hon. friend (Mr. Vien) as to the passage of this Order in Council is about right. The Acting Minister of Justice is usually very strong and clear in his reasoning on matters of law but I did not think he was very strong in saying that he could get a little authority here and a little there, go back to as many statutes as he liked and get an accumulation of authority, in order to pass an Order in Council. I do not think that is good law or reasoning. That is something that the courts guard against in this country. They say that your authority must be absolutely good before an Order in Council stands. It is not good in itself unless it is based on the authority of some statute. When a statute is passed giving the Governor in Council authority to pass an Order in Council in order to implement that statute, that authority is clear and is the mind of Parliament as expressed in that

statute. An Order in Council cannot issue under another statute. I am sure that the Acting Minister of Justice would not say that you could travel from that statute to some other statute and get supplementary authority from it to authorize the issue of an Order in Council. Every Order in Council must be based on some statutory authority and upon that statutory authority alone. I think we should all understand that the courts and constitution of the country, as well as the English courts for as far back as we have any records, have zealously protected the rights of Parliament and the people as against overreaching authority by Order in Council. The courts have always quashed proceedings under an Order in Council unless it was solidly based upon some parliamentary authority as expressed in the statute. If the minister says that these Orders in Council in connection with the coal and mineral lands in the Northwest were based upon the War Measures Act, I would certainly say tnat the authority was not good, and that it was straining the Act beyond any conceivable understanding Parliament had when it passed it to say that it was good enough to use as a basis for making Orders in Council with respect to mineral lands in the Northwest. I hope there is some other and better authority which enabled the minister to pass that Order in Council. If he is entirely without authority, it would be better to come here with a clause in this Bill enabling the Government to pass this title to the people who have a right to get it than to tell us that there is an Order in Council to confirm something that we know nothing about. I suppose this is all right. At the same time the .minister must not presume too much upon our confidence in him, and in the Government, in seeking to pass legislation without giving the proper information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend's doctrine is thoroughly sound an Order in Council is without value unless rooted, and very clearly rooted, in the authority of a statute.
I hope the hon. gentleman will continue to preach that doctrine to his followers from all parts of the country. But what I said was this: That an Order might rest upon one statute, or, indeed, might rest upon two, and if, to make the Order, in the body of it two statutes are invoked, then if either one is found to authorize it the Order stands; that is all I said. Consequently, those entrusted with-the responsibility of drafting recommendations and Orders in Council usually adopt the practice of in-

voking any authority that may be of assistance to support the Order intended. Therefore, it is possible that more than one statute was invoked in this case. The material before me, however, does not indicate that the War Measures Act was used, but would rather denote that it was passed under the regulatory power of the Forest Reserves and Parks Act. The War Measures Act might have been used; if it were I fancy it would be held to be a valid statute. But anyway the question does not arise now because the question before Parliament is, should these rights be granted, and should they be granted in a future case of a like character, because this legislation will confirm in any event?

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The minister told us that the Order in Council had not been passed under the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I understood him to say so a minute ago. If the minister now corrects me on that point I am ready to accept his correction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is wrong.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I asked the minister whether the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act gave the Government authority to pass the Order in Council of which we are now speaking. He answered me in the negative, and that is why, it .seems, legislation is now required.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Forest Reserves and Parks Act does not provide at all for the class of cases-this is what I have in mind and maybe the hon. gentleman misunderstood me-covered by this section. That is a class of cases that have arisen since the passing of the Act, viz:	It has
been discovered that there are certain other rights acquired before the passing of the Act which were not known to exist. The Bill does not exempt them from the provisions of the Bill providing for the creation of a park, but it is quite possible that the power of regulation comprised in the measure would enable the Governor in Council to do so. I do not say that it does not-it i-s quite possible it does-but whether it does or does not this legislation confirms what was done. And Parliament should consider is this: Is it proper that men who, prior to the establishment of the park, had acquired certain definite rights, should have those rights now confirmed? I do not know whether there are any other cases
than the three already dealt with, but there may be others, and in my humble judgment, there is no question about the propriety of confirming the rights in those cases. It seems to me that it would be simply legislating rights away to refuse to do so.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I quite agree, if the facts are as stated, that the owners of the mineral rights in these claims should receive back those rights. But outside of that question of fact there is a question of principle of which the leader of the Opposition was speaking a minute ago, and that is the question of the Government passing an Order in Council with no legal authority to do so, except that embodied in the War Measures Act. It is customary for the Government, when it passes an Order in Council, to recite in that Order the legislation on which it is based. Has the minister the Order in Council in this case before him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No. I have a memorandum with respect to it, but it is not definite in its terms.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The minister has not the Order in Council before him? Then it might be enlightening to read that Order in Council in order to determine on what authority it is based. If there is no statutory authority outside of the War Measures Act to justify such an Order in Council I think it is proper for hon. gentlemen on this side to bring to the attention of the Government the fact that it should not pass an Order in Council before having the necessary legislation. The remedy which was sought by the passing of Order in Council No. 2156, could easily have waited until the Government had submitted the necessary legislation to Parliament. I think it is a sound principle of British government to say that instead of passing an Order in Council without authority under the law, the Government should apply to Parliament for that authority. The Order in Council in this case is not valid, if it is not based on statutory authority, until it is ratified by Parliament. It seems to me that instead of passing an Order in Council, without any authority for so doing, it would be a more logical policy for the Government to come to the House and ask for an enactment that would provide the necessary remedy. In that way they would avoid having recourse to an illegal Order in Council. Surely, those who consented to the War Measures Act never thought that it would

be taken advantage of for the passing of such an Order in Council as the one we are now called upon to ratify.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended, agreed to.
On section 3-power given to expropriate lands for park purposes:

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: With respect to the expropriation of Indian lands. As I understand it, the Indians hold these lands at the present time by virtue of a treaty with the Government, and under the present Bill the minister is taking the right to expropriate Indian lands for park purposes, or other purposes if necessary. I would like to ask if the Government has a right to do that without the consent of the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There could be no-question, I think, as to the right of Parliament to do that generally speaking. As to the expediency of such a course, I should give an opinion in the negative. That is to say, Parliament would be very careful indeed not to adopt any general policy of expropriation as to Indian reserves. Under the present law it is necessary to establish' expropriatory powers, for Indian reserves. For railroad or public works purposes, or even for roads, that power exists to-day; the only question that arises is, should the power be extended to cover the case of necessary additions to parks?
There is a case in point at the present time: An island in the St. Lawrence near the town of Morrisburg in which a certain Indian tribe acquired rights about a hundred years ago. My information may be wrong and I hope the hon, member for Dundas (Mr. Casselman) is present, but I understand that no one has been living on that island for years; it has been used by some company, although I do not wish to speak with too great certainty. However, it is very desirable in the public interest that it be acquired for park purposes. I think I am safe in saying .that any title the Indians may have is rather cloudy, but whatever interest they may have they will be amply compensated for and t,fiere will be no loss to the tribe. There is a very strong desire on the part of the Parks Branch and on the part of the public most nearly concerned that this island be acquired and made a bird sanctuary and park. That is most clearly the purpose it should be used for, but unless the amendment is made wide enough to cover it no action can be taken to that end.
I wish to assure the hon. member and the House generally that in my judgment

Parliament should be very rautious, indeed, in passing expropriatory legislation applicable to Indian Reserves. I have had occasion to give some thought to the question in relation to another measure, and where the expropriation is for merely general purposes-farming and the like-I question very much whether Parliament should pass such legislation; but inasmuch as this is not of a general character, and cannot be said to be an invasion of Indian Reserves in any substantial sense at all, I do not think we should hesitate to enact the legislation.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
How many Dominion
parks are there now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am not prepared to say how many there are. There are a considerable number in the various provinces, and there is an intention to increase the number. The value to the country of these parks is becoming more and more obvious as years go by. The amount of money left in the country because of their existence runs now into millions of dollars annually.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Government is now asking for power to expropriate. Has the Government any definite policy as to the lands that it will expropriate in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: - The only case touching Indian lands is this island. It is a small island in the St. Lawrence-I do not know just the size of it. That is the only case we have in mind at the present time.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Would it not be better for the Government to specify the land and to come before Parliament each time it wants to expropriate? The matter is never of such an urgent character that we could not wait until the next session of Parliament before such power is granted, and then the House and the country at large would have an opportunity to give their reasons why such expropriation should not take place in the ordinary course.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Parliament will have
that opportunity. If the power is right, that is a question of principle; but the particular appropriation would be decided when the Estimate for it is before the House. Even though this Bill pass, the question of expropriating this particular island will come up when the item for its expropriation is before the Committee in the Estimates. Therefore each individual case must necessarily come before Parliament

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: For what purpose are those Dominion parks established?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: For Dominion parks.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What ds the purpose of a Dominion park?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not know that any words could do other than obscure the very plain meaning of the term "Dominion parks."

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have a Dominion Park in Montreal, for instance; that is for amusement purposes. I suppose the minister is not establishing parks for amusement purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I really think the hon. member understands what a park is for as well as I do. I hope he does not question me as if I were the father of something that is improper. These Dominion parks were established many years ago, virtually all that are established now, under a Government to which the hon. member was not at all unfriendly. But our Dominion parks
are for the purpose of instruction, amusement and recreation, for the purpose of attracting tourists, for sightseeing, and all such purposes. For example, we have one park where there are now between three and four thousand buffalo-the only herd of wild buffalo in the world. I do not know that one could say that it is purely an .amusement to watch our wild buffalo; it is instructive and highly interesting.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is also dangerous.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Then we have our
Rocky Mountain parks where tourists gather. A golf course has been established and is being very much improved. A vast amount of money is being collected from those best able to pay it. With reference to what the hon. member has said, every expropriation is just on the same footing as this. For instance, under our Expropriation Act now, for any building we wish to erect, we can expropriate, but no one would ever suggest that we must come to Parliament and have a Bill passed enabling us to expropriate each lot that we may want in each town in Canada. No one knows better than the hon. member how much time is taken in getting Bills through Parliament and how much time is wasted. I do not think Parliament would ever get through its work if for every piece of land the Government wanted, it had to come to Parliament with a Bill. We take the general power and then each case must be passed upon by Parliament in the Estimates. That has been the practice for decades, and there is no variation here.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Are there any such parks in Quebec, or Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick?
. Mr. MEIGHEN:	I think I am safe in
saying that there are Dominion parks in all of the provinces named. I cannot say that I am familiar with each case. I know that at present we have in contemplation the establishment of a park at Annapolis Royal in Nova Scotia. I think that last session a Bill was brought down that had (to do with the establishment of a bird sanctuary on the St. Lawrence in Quebec. That is of course, a park.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: On Bonaventure Island.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The park at
Annapolis Royal is a very small one; it is just a bit of historic ground near the town of Annapolis. If the minister is going into the park business, there are in Nova Scotia places where it would be of great ' advantage to have a public reservation of

land for that purpose. These lands in western Nova Scotia and also in eastern Nova Scotia belong to the provincial Government. There is not very much timber on some of them, but there are lakes and streams and many beautiful spots are to be found. I do not see why Nova Scotia should not, as well as the Western Provinces, participate to some extent in this expenditure on parks. I could show my hon. friend a place in western Nova Scotia where a large block of land could be expropriated from the province at a very small price, for a Dominion park. In my constituency, there is a tract of 20,000 acres of hardwood, such as birch, maple and beech, not valuable as timber at all, but the whole area is dotted with lakes and streams and would be a magnificent place for recreation and fishing and for the preservation of game. I should like the minister to look into this matter. I am in favour of public parks. I think the reservations we have made at Banff and other places in Western Canada are an advantage to us all, and we are very proud of them. At the same time, I think Eastern Canada should, to some extent, participate in that expenditure, and as the minister has taken power to expropriate lands belonging to the provinces, it would be quite possible to take this strip under this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
quite right that it would be to the advantage, not only of Nova Scotia, but of the Dominion, if in his province any property more suitable for park purposes than any other were made a park. I just happened to mention Annapolis Royal because only this afternoon the subject was brought to my attention. This, however, must be kept in mind, that while the establishment of parks has gone on with to a considerable degree in the West, that is attributable chiefly to the fact that the Dominion owned these lands in the West and did not need to acquire them. Consequently, the cost, of establishment of parks was not so great. My province of Manitoba, although we owned the lands, has no Dominion parks, nor, I believe, has Saskatchewan. Alberta has, and quite a large area of that province is set aside, and very properly so, for Dominion parks. British Columbia, which owns its resources, has acquired property for a park on Vancouver island, and a provincial Government which owns its own resources could give great assistance to the establishment of parks by making provision for the land.
I do not attach very great importance to the clause giving us power to expropriate

provincial Crown lands. I presume it is intended for small pieces of land perhaps essential as an addition to a present park. Certainly, I would hesitate before utilizing this power as applied to provincial Crown lands.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Might I suggest to the minister that this clause appears more drastic than it is in reality after the explanation given by him? As regards bird sanctuaries, T have a personal knowledge of what t.,ok place during last year regarding legislation on that subject which was brought down a: a former session. In that case, the Dominion Government sent one of the officers of the Department of the Interior, Mr. Hewitt, to Quebec, and by making arrangements with the Department of Crown Lands, he obtained, without any expropriation taking place, the control of Bird Rock and part of Bonaventure Island and also Perce Rock, as bird sanctuaries. If the minister leaves in the Bill this expropriatory power he may create the impression that he may really expropriate what belongs to a province, when it is a matter of arrangement between this Government and the provincial Government. The minister should, therefore, find other phraseology which would cover the point. I understand that, as regards the Indians, the Government proceeds by way of expropriation, and in that case the Government is proceeding against its own wards, but with the provinces the matter is different. I am not referring to the western provinces, where the lands belong to the Dominion, but to the provinces where the lands belong to the provinces, as with the Crown lands in Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Federal Government has no right to expropriate provincial property. In the British North America Act property belonging to the Federal Government is enumerated, and property belonging to the provincial governments is enumerated. His Majesty, as representing the provinces, owns what is enumerated in that list, and I do not think the Federal Government could take expropriation proceedings against the provinces. I think the minister will admit that the Federal Government, in the name of His Majesty, certainly could not take proceedings against His Majesty as represented by a provincial Government. The minister said he did not want to be suspected of any evil designs or of being the father of a very bad scheme. Personally I have never suspected him of anything of that kind, for he is above suspicion, and always has been. He has never

given the Opposition any reason to suspect him. This Bill is very important in a way. In the province of Quebec, for instance, parks have already been- established by the Provincial Government; there is the park in the county of Charlevoix. Suppose that under this section the Federal Government decided to establish a national park where this provincial park now is, would the minister claim that this section gave him the right to expropriate ? It would lead at once to a clash between the Federal and Provincial Governments. 1 have noticed a general tendency in all legislation brought down by the minister to infringe upon provincial rights, and this certainly would be such an infringement. I submit, this section is absolutely unconstitutional, because it gives the Federal Government the right to expropriate the property of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would not like to subscribe to the hon. gentleman's law. It seems to me that expropriatory power now exists with regard to provincial lands, with relation to a railway, for instance. But as a matter of general principle, not of law, but of practice, I am in accord with the hon. member. My attention had not been specially drawn to these words in the Bill previously. I rather apprehend that the province of Ontario may also have some interest in the island in the St. Lawrence to which I referred, that interest being mixed with or added to the interest of the Indians, and it is likely that that was in the mind of the draftsman of the Bill. I would not like to exercise the power of expropriation so far as the interests of the province are concerned, but I do hot think it could be said to be interfering with provincial rights to the alarming extent the hon. member would have us believe; for you may depend upon it that any province in the Dominion would be very glad for us to expropriate lands in the province for the purpose of a Dominion park. At the same time, I do not think we are going to suffer by leaving out the clause providing for the [DOT]expropriation of provincial lands, and I therefore move in amendment :
That the, words " whether it be that of His Majesty in the right of any province, or of the Indians " be deleted and the words " including the lands of Indians" be substituted therefor.
Then, if we cannot make an arrangement with the province there will be no park.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You can always make an arrangement with a province in a matter of public interest. The minister has referred to an island that is in dispute as between the Indian reserve and the province.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Indians have some right in it.	.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We have a similar
case in the province of Quebec. There is a small island in front of the Caughnawaga reserve which is claimed by the Indians as part of the reserve, and which is claimed also by the provincial Government. There has been quite a dispute, over it, and I am not quite sure but that a judgment concerning it was given recently.
