I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and the Government the altogether inadequate salaries paid to judges not only of the County Court but also of the Supreme Court of British Columbia. Speaking at present particularly in reference to the County Court judges, this is a matter that has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice on many occasions, and we have



frequently had promises of consideration and expressions of much sympathy, but very little action. I should be pleased to have an expression of opinion from the Acting Minister of Justice on the subject, and also a statement as to the possibility before the conclusion of the session of an increase in salary of the County Court judges. The County Court judges in the city of Vancouver sit constantly and do considerable work, and I remember having given to the Minister of Justice a statement showing that 365 cases were being handled by two judges in fhe course of a Fall session. That is an exceptionally heavy list, including some highly important cases, the money involved in some cases amounting to a good many thousand dollars and much higher than in cases tried in some of the other courts in Canada. A salary of $3,000 is not sufficient for a County Court judge, and I would like the minister to give us some idea as to the intention of the Government in this regard.

I wish to say a word on this point with regard to the judges of Prince Edward Island. The Supreme Court judges there are receiving $300 a year less than similar judges in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The duties of a judge in Prince Edward Island are just as important and require just as much intelligence, application, and every other qualification demanded of like judges in the other provinces. In Prince Edward Island there are only three judges while in the other provinces there is a much larger number, and because there are fewer judges in the Island they have just as much work and probably more. At the same time there exists this anomaly, that the County Court judges are receiving the same amount of salary in Prince Edward Island as those in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and other provinces. Why should the Supreme Court judges be penalized? I just wish to bring this matter to the attention of the minister as perhaps he might consider an increase in the salaries Qf these judges.

The hon. member (Mr. Stevens) spoke of 365 cases. That is an exception and might not occur again in several years. The question is, what is the average? As regards the proposal to increase these judges salaries, I understand the judges pay no income tax. Surely a judge receiving $5,000 to $7,000 should have sufficient interest in the State to pay an income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), supported

by the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Mclsaac) urges the wisdom of increasing the salaries of County Court judges. The necessity of an increase of salary to County Court judges has been impressed upon the Government ever since I assumed the office of Acting Minister of Justice, and doubtless some time before that event, which is now six months old. The question is not confined to County Court judges. If there is any class of judges in Canada for whose cause there are not ardent advocates for an increase of salary, I have yet to learn what bench it is. Every bench in the Dominion, I think, has had its case advanced and urged, deputation after deputation having waited upon myself and other ministers, and the subject generally has begn canvassed most thoroughly in recent months. There- are several features of the problem that might be brought to the attention of the Committee. In the case of County Court judges the income now received for their duties is not uniform by any means. The senior judge is entitled to certain emoluments and the junior judge also in a somewhat lesser scale. So that while $3,000 is the nominal salary, there are cases where even that salary is increased, those cases being chiefly in large cities.
I do not think that applies to the County Court of British Columbia. That is the peculiar position they are in.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are eases where that is not the nominal salary, but in nearly all cases, I think in all, the emolument is raised above the nominal salary by Surrogate Court and other fees.
Not in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it is. That is worth inquiry on the part of the hon. member. Perhaps I am wrong. But generally, if not universally speaking, it is, and the total emolument is brought to something within the range of $4,000, and in some cases even somewhat beyond that. When I considered the question this fact presented itself to my mind, that by reason of the system which the British North America Act laid down-constitution of the office by the province, and appointment and salary made and paid by the Dominion-there had grown up a condition by which there were far too many judges, particularly of our county courts and district courts. I addressed a communication to the Attorneys General of the several provinces, intimating that such was the case and asking that they

give attention to the question of so rearranging the judiciary as to provide for an ultimate reduction of the number of County Court judges. The province of Ontario has responded* and I believe a statute is now in force by which the junior judges will be almost entirely done away with upon retirement or death of the present holders of those offices.
Other provinces have now under consideration-whether it will be favourable or not I cannot say-something along the same line. I am in hopes that the process will become more and more all Canadian before it ceases, because, if it becomes general enough, the problem of judicial salaries will be more easily solved. As a. consequence of my oonvicion that there were too many judges, particularly on that bench, I have not felt it my duty as acting minister to recommend the filling of certain vacancies that now exist. Furthermore, coming to the other bench, the King's Bench, as it is usually called, the Supreme and superior courts in other provinces, a condition of affairs obtains that has caused considerable irritation. In the Maritime and Western Provinces the salaries of judges in these courts are something less than they are in Ontario and Quebec. That condition is accentuated in the province of Prince Edward Island. Whether or not there was originally justification for that discrimination may be open to question. It would appear to be arguable that there was. But, at all events, the reason for that discrimination has, in my opinion, become progressively less as these other provinces have developed and as the litigation that comes before the judges of these provinces has be* come more and more technical, more considerable in amount and more varied as to, the questions of law presented. That is a matter that hon.. members will have to keep in mind in discussing the problem. It appeared to me to be my duty to collect all the facts available, to put them into presentable, terse and tangible form, and to leave the problem in general for the consideration of the minister of the department (Mr. Doherty) upon his return. It has not been known until now-it is not known now-when that return will be possible, but there is no reason to fear that it will be so long deferred as to put it out oi his power to deal with this question favourably or unfavourably this session. If his opinion on his return is that he cann#t ueal with the question this session, as he may be advised, then I do not think I should
147i
enter upon its consideration in a practical way because it seems to me to be one that eminently is for the consideration of the minister himself. Should it transpire that he will not be able to return for the subsequent portion of this session, then it will be for the Government to decide whether or not the problem should be dealt with on the recommendation of the acting minister.

Do not the
county judges, in addition to their salaries, earn considerable emoluments from commissions and special investigations which would in themselves average a pretty good salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what I referred to in my remarks. I do not think much is made out of commissions or investigations. The extra amount which I referred to was that which they actually received from Surrogate Court fees. The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) says that that does not apply in his province. He may be correct but, generally speaking, it does apply.
Do they not act as commissioners, or conduct special investigations, and do they not earn something in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There have been Superior and county court judges, I suppose, who have acted in that way, but the earnings of a single judge from that source would not do very much for the other men who had not been favoured with these investigations.

Will this resolution apply
to the appointment of judges in Saskatchewan? There are several vacancies, and some of them should be filled.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, this resolution refers only to the province of British Columbia and follows the provincial enactment which constitutes the judicial district of Nanaimo. It appears that the extent of territory there is such that it cannot be attended to by one judge, particularly in view of the very great increase 5 p.m. in population and the development of coal mining - in the northern part of the district. This resolution does not refer to Saskatchwan. Letters were addressed to the various provinces asking them to consider the question of reduction. I am in hopes that these letters will still be fruitful in the case of 'Saskatchewan to enable the present judges appointed to be so distributed as to take care

of the vacancies to which the hon. member refers.

I would like to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Justice to the discrepancy between the salaries paid to Superior. Court judges in -the western provinces and those paid in the East. Whatever ground there may have been for that distinction when it was created I cannot see that there is any reason for it now. The western provinces are provinces. The standard of the legal profession in the West will compare very favourably with that of the other provinces. It seems to me that the questions involved in litigation are just as important in the West ns they are elsewhere. It .is not altogether a question of the amount of time that the judges devote to the performance of their duties in the various provinces. Once these men are appointed they cannot or should not engage in any other business. They are absolutely deprived of the right of practising their profession. In short, the whole of their time must be devoted to carrying on the business of their positions as justices of the Superior court. On 'behalf of the western bench, I submit that this difference in salary which has existed for some time should be straightened out at once and that all the judges of the superior court throughout the Dominion of Canada, irrespective of province, should be placed upon the same footing. I would like very much if the acting minister would take this -matter into his earnest and careful consideration this session and see if he cannot remedy that discrimination and put all -these judges "on an equal footing. I am sure that all the members of this House would be very glad to have the acting minister review the situation in regard to judges' salaries throughout Canada.

I wish once more to bring to the notice of the acting minister what we have been advocating here for a number of years. I remember in the old days of the Laurier Government we used to talk about this subject just as much as we do now, and we used to advocate an increase, particularly in the salaries of the county court judges. Within the last few years we have often brought this matter to the attention of the present Minister of Justice.
I can readily understand that the Acting Minister of Justice would hesitate before starting a new policy as to the increase of salaries; but I think the minister himself (Mr. Doherty) was several

times inclined seriously to the advancement of the salaries of the County Court judges, and I think last year he was very much disposed to augment those salaries. The reason now given by the acting minister for not adopting such a course is that there is a tendency to a re-organization of the districts and of the courts, and to have a smaller number of judges. That re-organization may come about, but it may be a very slow process, and it may result in great hardship to those judges who have been struggling along for a great many years on small salaries. The high cost of living affects a judge just as much as anybody else. Civil servants have been granted an increase, those engaged in the ordinary industries of the country are getting their salaries raised; nearly everybody in fact has had his stipend raised. Ordinarily speaking, men can engage in other branches of work in order to add to'their salaries; but under our laws the judge is told that he cannot and must not engage in any other pursuit. He is not even allowed to be a director of a board where he can be paid $20 a month, or something of that kind; he is not allowed to engage in anything except the administration of the law. That is as it should be, but when we cut off every other source of supply to a man and demand his entire attention and the whole of his powers in the administration of the law, the responsibility devolves upon us of giving him a sufficient salary, we should see to it that he is placed beyond necessity and beyond poverty. Now we have not added a cent to the salary of the judge, although the purchasing ^ower of a dollar has been cut in two. It is therefore a matter of serious consideration for the Government, and particularly for the Minister of Justice, to see that these judges are properly provided for. I need not tell the Acting Minister of Justice, or the Committee, what a serious and important [DOT] thing it is that our judges shoul-cl be put beyond covetousness, or the temptation of looking for money elsewhere. We can say the same thing for our judges in every part of Canada that we can say about our own judges in Nova Scotia, that not a shadow of impropriety has crept in in connection with the administration of justice. We have always been proud of our judges in Nova Scotia, who are absolutely beyond suspicion, and I am sure the same thing is true of the judges of every other province. We should provide for the conti nu-

ance of that condition as far as we can, by giving a proper salary. Would it not be possible for the Department of Justice for the present to relieve the situation by adding to the salaries of these judges, and then, under any policy of re-construction those Judges who are superfluous might go out, such arrangements being made for them as might meet the necessities of the case? If we wait foT re-organization too long a period may elapse before a remedy is provided, and a great deal of unnecessary hardship may have been suffered by these gentlemen.
I trust that the department-when the minister returns to this country, or even before that- will be able to meet the need in these very important cases.
As regards my own province it contains eighteen counties and there are only seven county court judges, so that I do not think there would be very much chance for reducing the number of judges in Nova Scotia. There may be, but I think all the judges are pretty well employed. The county court judge in my own locality, that is . district No. 7, is a very busy man, working continuously and without any let-up at all. Every day there is some case being tried before him, and yet he only receives the very meagre salary of $3,000. He is obliged to live in the city of Sydney, where living is just as expensive as in Toronto, Montreal, or any of the large centres, and hon. gentlemen can readily understand how difficult it is for a man to live in a city where everything is dear on a salary of $3,000, and yet be obliged to live in the style, and with the surroundings for himself and his family that a judge must maintain in order to do credit to the position which he occupies. I do not know very much about the conditions in other provinces, but ajs to the Nova Scotia judges supplementing their earnings from any other source, that is not possible; they get nothing out of probate business, and no other income besides their bare salaries. The Acting Minister of Justice is aware that there is an agitation in respect of the Supreme Court judges as well as the County Court judges in Nova Scotia. We in Nova Scotia pride ourselves on being a very old province, and one which has been noted for the very high status of the judges in our Supreme Court. They are men very highly versed in the science of the law, and we have a Bench to-day that is the equal, man for man, with any other set of judges in the country. I say that without the desire to cast the slightest reflection on any other court.
I am sorry to know that the judges of Nova Scotia are not paid the same salaries, for example, as the judges of Manitoba. Now we are a very much older province and of equal importance in every respect-not any more, but just as important-and I cannot very well see why a judge of the Supreme Court of Manitoba should be receiving a larger salary than a judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. -

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the judges in the Maritime Provinces and in the Western Provinces should receive the same salary.
The Chief Justice of Manitoba receives $8,000 a year-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal.

-and the puisne judges receive $7,000 a year. Of course, there are two courts in Manitoba, whereas in Nova Scotia there is but one. That is to say our Supreme Court in Nova Scotia does the work which two courts do in Manitoba; we have only the one set of judges for the Court of Appeal and for the Circuit Court. In New Brunswick, and in the other provinces, there is a Circuit Court and a Court of Appeal; in Nova Scotia the judges do the Circuit Court work, and also constitute themselves a Court of Appeal. I think that is a reason why they should be pafd a higher salary. The minister will see, if he compares Manitoba with Nova Scotia, that the population is about the same; I think ours is a little more; and if he will inquire into the amount of legal business, I think he will find that there is more of it in Nova Scotia. As to the expense of the administration of justice, the minister will find that if he makes inquiry that the same work is costing at least about thirty per cent more in Manitoba than it is costing .in Nova Scotia. I think our judges should be put upon the same footing as the judges of the Superior Court of Quebec and the Superior Court of Ontario, and be paid the same salary. I know of no justification at all for the difference. The laws are about the same throughout the whole Dominion -certainly the criminal laws are exactly the same, and commercial law is about the same-and if the amount involved in the cases that come into court is to be taken into consideration the biggest case that was ever tried in Canada was heard in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. That was the famous lawsuit between the Dominion Steel Company and the Dominion Coal Company before they amalgamated. I do

"not know how many millions of money were [DOT]involved in the suit, but it is the largest -case that was ever tried in the Dominion. Large cases of that kind come up all the time and require the very best legal talent that we can produce in the province.
I think the minister will approve my statement that the province of Nova Scotia has produced some very excellent lawyers in fact, this House will bear me out. Sir John Thompson, at one time Minister of Justice and Prime Minister, was one of our judged of whom we have good reason to be proud, and our present Prime Minister, who is a very excellent lawyer, is also a native of Nova Scotia. The judges-of our Supreme Court are men of the highest possible eminence in their profession, and I do not think they should .look upon themselves as being inferior to other judges serving the same Government and doing similar work in the other provinces. There is no other way of looking at it-the clear implication is that the Government thinks they are not deserving of the same salary, otherwise they ' would receive it. I am not aware if the minister has any scheme in view for dealing with the salaries of Supreme Court judges , throughout the country as well as with those of the County Court judges, but I think he should hasten to see that there is no disparity in their salaries and so remove any ground for complaint in that regard. I am sure that as long as our people find the administration of. justice as pure and capable as it is now they will not begrudge the payment of proper salaries to their Supreme Court judges.

I would like to correct a mistaken impression of the Acting Minister of Justice. The County Court judges of British Columbia-in fact, all the judges- receive no Surrogate Court fees. Their position is not only unfair in comparison with the salaries paid to judges in other provinces, but the difference is accentuated, and I desire to impress it as strongly as possible upon the attention of the minister. I would also remind him of the fact that the benchers of the Law iSociety of British Columbia recently filed a very strong indorsement of the suggested increase of salary, and I hope the matter will not be left over another session, even if the Minister of Justice should not return during this session.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Committee should not get the impression that because the judges in certain provinces do not get surrogate court fees there is on that account discrimination against them; that is far

from the case. The Dominion fees are the same everywhere. But if the province of Ontario decides, for example, that instead of having other officials appointed at salary to do surrogate court work they will appoint a Supreme Court judge to do it and pay him a thousand dollars a year, that adds that much to his salary; if British Columbia, as against that decides to appoint separate officials, that is British Columbia's own affair.

That is scarcely a good argument. For this reason: The Dominion pays the Supreme Court judges for services rendered; the time of those judges is fully occupied in their court work and they have no time for outside work now, if one of those judges gives a portion of his time to the province in return for a salary provided by the province, and the rest of his time to the Dominion, the minister cannot argue that the other judges have only themselves to blame if they do not receive additional pay. Their time is fully occupied in court work-more than occupied in many cases. But in Ontario and some of the other provinces the Supreme Court' judges give a portion of their time to other duties.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surrogate court work
is court work just the same as any other similar work is court work. No case has been brought to my attention where the Dominion has refused to appoint sufficient judges to take care of the work. It is the province's own affair if it gives to other people work that is properly judges' work; and that province cannot be heard then to complain that its judges are not treated fairly by the Dominion because we do not give more salary to them, for the same salary is paid to all Supreme Court judges.

My hon. friend still
argues that they get surrogate court fees, we must not run aw^ay with 'the idea that they are getting more than $3,000. I say that out British Columbia judges get $3,000 and no more, and that that salary is inadequate.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be, but that is entirely aside from the point of discrimination. There is no discrimination whatsoever; w>e pay all our Supreme Court judges the same salary.
It is not discrimination if the Dominion gives them a good salary.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is another ground altogether. We pay them all the same sal-

ary. If the province does not add to their salaries for additional court work, but appoints other persons for the purpose, then that province cannot be heard to complain against the Dominion that we discriminate against its judges- There is no ground for any allegation of discrimination. I am not saying that there is no ground for an allegation of inadequate salary.

Does the minister think it sound policy to allow Federal judges to discharge other duties than those the iaw has fixed for them, such as surrogate work on account of the province? It seems to me that the judges appointed by the Federal Government should be limited in their functions as described by the statute, and should not be allowed to exercise any other functions and receive therefor emoluments from the provinces. As a policy it seems to me it should commend itself to the minister

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A judge is appointed to do such work, necessarily of a legal or judicial character, as may be assigned to him by the Dominion or by the province. If the province assigns to him eertaiu work, it is his duty under the Act to perform it. To say that he should not do anything except what the Dominion gives him to do-I scarcely understand those terms.

I will explain them. Jurisdiction in the organization of the various tribunals is vested in the local legislatures. When the organization * of a tribunal is effected by a provincial Act, the Federal Government appoints the judges. We fix the salary and we pay it. We should pay judges such salaries as will make them independent of any other influence and allow them to live without having to exercise any [DOT] other functions for which? they would receive pay from the provinces.

My hon. friend is not familiar with the practice in Ontario. In Ontario, the judges are well qualified to deal with Surrogate Court work, and in most counties the fees would not be large enough to warrant the appointment of a separate judge for that particular work. As the Acting Minister of Justice said, Ontario amended the County Court Judges Act last year, and in future County Court judges will receive $1,000 from, the province as compensation for their services in doing Surrogate Court work and work under other statutes. There are certain large counties, such as York, Carleton and Wentworth, in which the judges will receive more than $1,000. I am not familiar with the position of County Court judges in other provinces,
but in Ontario, after the junior judges are done away with, County Court judges will receive from the province at least $1,000, which will increase their salary by so much.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Making $4,000 all together.

If- the minister finds it impossible to make an arrangement with the Saskatchewan Government to redistribute the judges to cover the vacancies, will he recommend the appointment of judges for those vacancies? There are, in the southwestern part of the province, two new districts, and Cypress, which is the seat of a district a hundred miles square, has only two terms of the court per annum. People are compelled to come into the town and stay for weeks waiting for trials, and on the other hand Judge Smith, who goes over from Swift Current, has more than ninety miles to travel by auto, and if the roads are bad in the winter, he has to travel 270 miles to get around by train. Therefore, I do not think the Government are saving any money and these people are being greatly inconvenienced Iby not having -a resident judge in that district.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be useless on my part to make a promise, because it is probable I shall not be acting in this capacity at the time for its fulfilment. I am not sure, at all events, whether Saskatchewan will be able to make the redistribution which has been suggested to me, although I have some reason to hope it will. But if it should not, there is an alternative. A subjudicial district might be named which would give the district affected, if in an outlying part, such an organization, with perhaps only one officer, as would enable it to secure a more prompt and less expensive service of process and so on. That has been suggested as likely to take place in at least one province, thereby overcoming much of the difficulty. If that should be done in Saskatchewan, the hon. member's point will be met, but if no other way-and this Government is not by any means sole dictator of the situation-is opened up by the province wheTeby this can be taken care of without appointing new judges, and if a district needs a judge, certainly a recommendation will be made. I understand there is very considerable inconvenience now which might be avoided by a better redistribution of the judges by the creation of a subjudicial district, but if that is not done, then it seems that a recommendation will have to be made.

Have the districts to
which the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Argue) refers been created by the local legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
This year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There have been two
vacancies for a year or two which we have not filled because we felt there were sufficient judges.
Has a new district been created in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The district is created
already by the province.

I ain glad to hear the Acting Minister of Justice say that one province at least has responded to his suggestion that there should be co-ordination with a view of getting more efficiency in judicial work, and I am glad that province is Ontario, of the Bar of which I am a member. I think I can say on behalf of the members of the Bar that -they entirely approve of the new Act of the Ontario Legislature by which junior judges are to be absorbed as vacancies occur. As the case stands now, the two judges in a county, senior and junior, get $6,000, and it would be far better if the senior judge were paid $5,000 so as to give him a decent income rather than that the work should be divided as it is now, because in many counties, we all know, there is not enough work to keep one man, who is industrious and has any system, thoroughly busy, much less is there sufficient for two judges to do. When the minister is considering the whole question, I would ask him to make a further suggestion that districts should be made for the smaller counties so that one judge could attend to one or two, or perhaps three counties. I know of three counties which one judge could very well attend to, and he could be given a large proportion of the remuneration of the three judges who are now supposed to do that work.	It is essential, if
the laws are to- be well administered, that judges have the respect of the people, and they should be paid adequate salaries, or else the best members of the Bar will not be willing to accept such positions. The County Court judges have very important work to do. In Ontario, a County Court judge, on account of increased jurisdiction given him by the province, can deal with many cases which formerly took up the time of a Supreme Court judge travelling at assizes. Even with all this extra work,

many of them would be better off and happier if they had more work to do, but they should be paid far more than they receive at present, and I hope an ascending scale will be adopted so that these judges will not feel the high cost of living as acutely as they do now. They cannot keep up their position with -the merchants and wealthy men of the towns in which they live, and that should not be the case. The idea of judicial remuneration is that a judge should not be thought to be inferior to the best class of citizens in the town in which he is. That is impossible at present with a judge getting only $3,000 a year, even if he gets something more for surrogate court work. The surrogate judge is not appointed by the Dominion but by the province, and the whole judicial work is distributed by the province. Therefore, the Dominion, apart from its good offices here, in asking for co-ordination, has nothing to do with *the particular work of, a judge, because, according to the British North America Act, all the Dominion Government has to deal with in this regard is the appointment of the judge; the rest is left to the province. I am glad Ontario is leading as regards the work of co-ordination and the saving of judicial effort, and I hope the other provinces will follow suit.

I agree that these judges are underpaid and that they should receive a substantial increase in salary, but under this resolution I do not see that we can get very much relief for them. I should like to inquire whether, in the event of legislation being introduced in regard to the judges of -the superior, county, and district courts, an increase in their salaries will be one of the matters taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it certainly will be.

I should like to say a word for the judges of the rural districts of the province of Quebec, who occupy a similar position to that of the county court judges in the province of Ontario, except that they have a little higher salary. A rural district judge in the province of Quebec receives $5,000 a year. Under the new system which has been adopted, these judges are called to Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, and even Sherbrooke, to help in the -administration of justice in those congested districts, and I do not see why they should not be put on a footing of equality with the judges of -the superior court of Montreal and Quebec. These judges are certainly handicapped by the
I

high cost of living. I am glad to hear that the acting minister has considered the whole question and that it will be dealt with on the return of the minister (Mr. Doherty) from Europe. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mow-at) has spoken of the legislation recently adopted by the Ontario Legislature. He might have added that many years ago, under the Mowat government, I think, the Ontario government finding the salaries of the judges of the higher courts in Ontario to be inadequate, supplemented their salaries by a yearly vote of $17000. This vote is still taken yearly, so that a superior court judge in the province of Ontario receives $1,000 more than he would receive in the province of Quebec. This shows that the people of Ontario have been more liberal to the judiciary than other provinces, and it seems to me the Dominion Government' should do what this one province has done. This additional $1,000 was granted under the pretext-because it was only a pretext-that in addition to their official functions they had to administer the Controverted Elections Act. The real reason was that the salaries of the judges were inadequate. I have not seen the memorandum addressed to the Acting Minister of Justice by the judiciary, but I know that it has been in circulation of late, and in view of the position the judges occupy in society, and having regard also to the independence of the judiciary, for my part I would look favourably upon a reasonable increase in their salaries. .
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Meighen thereupon moved to introduce Bill No. 104, founded on the resolution.
Resolution agreed to and Bill read a first time.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 81, to amend the Interpretation Act.-
Explain.

This is an item dealing with salaries. There may not be an item before the House at any time that will go specifically to the point I wish to bring to the notice of the President - of the Council, and I may mention the matter now. This is part of the Civil Service Estimates and these men, I suppose, are within the zone of the Civil Service. For that reason I do not think I transgress any rule^ in referring to another branch of the .service in connection with .this item. The question of a bonus to civil servants has been before the House once or twice this session, and I understand that the bonus was given by .way of an increase in salary pending the legislation about which the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Maclean) spoke to-day. I suppose that that legisla-ion of the Civil Service, will possibly end in an increase of salaries to at least the inside service, and I hope it will cover all servants, whether inside or outside as far as may be necessary. This bonus, as I am informed, was paid to keep matters in equilibrium until the general Act was passed, and if one person gets the benefit of it I submit that all in the service should get it. We have officers in this House working around the different parts of the building who must be here during the session. It is true that during a few months of the year they are not here, but they aTe men who have been in* attendance here for several years, as long as twenty and twenty-five years, and who have become in every way adapted to this sort of work. They have no other employment and I submit that this bonus that was paid to other civil servants should also be paid to them. There are not very many of them and they should be fairly dealt with. I think the President of the Council should immediately take steps to ascertain who they are and what should, fall to them, and gladden their hearts by giving them what they should receive. There should be no discrimination or distinction simply because these persons are sessional clerks or people who attehd during the session. They are to all intents and purposes civil -servants, who have been here for many years and who will, I sup*

pose, be here for the rest of their natural lives.
The point raised by the hon. member hardly arrises upon the estimate now before the committee.
I admit that.

But out of respect to my hon. friend's suggestion I may say that the bonuses were granted under two limitations, one being that they, applied only to those receiving salaries of $1,800 or less, because-and I am- speaking now of the bonus given by Order in Council-it was felt that the high cost of living bore more severely on those receiving smaller salaries than on those who were in receipt of higher salaries. Another limitation was that it applied only to those continually in the service. I presume that is the point my hon. friend has in mind in referring to the sessional clerks, who are not paid on a basis, of yearly allowance. I do not know whether they were in view when the form of Order in Council was determined upon. I shall bring my hon. friend's representation in this matter to the attention of my colleagues. It was considered that those who worked for the Government two or three months in the year but were not in Government employ longer should hardly be paid a bonus on the same basis as those in the Government employ the whole time. I may say that the whole matter, so far as the future is concerned, will come up for review when the re-classification of which the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke to-day, comes before the House for consideration.

I am not bringing this matter up for the mere sake of talking about it. I want something done for these people, and hope the President of the Council will take it seriously into consideration and bring it before his colleagues. I trust that no mere lack of covering this point by Order in Council will stand in the way of doing justice to these people who" are very excellent servants of the Government, because the Order in Council can be amended, or extended, or a new Order in Council passed. It would not take long to do it. My hon. friend has a very expert knowledge of how these things are done, and can just put his foot on the wheel at any time and grind one out in very short order. So that the lack of power to do it through want of legislation is no excuse for the President of the Council or the.Government.
There is an increase of fifteen hundred odd dollars. What does it consist of?
It consists of $1,000 additional amount payable to deputy minister and comptroller, just the same increase as is given to all other deputies. The other increases, I believe, are statutory increases.

What relations, if any, exist between provincial governments and this Government in regard to the services of the Mounted Police? I understood there was to be a change by which in some provinces they were to come within the jurisdiction of the province, more especially since governments have been established in different parts' of the West and the jurisdiction of ordinary civil and criminal administration of justice has come largely within the purview of the provinces. Are we keeping up the same staff or number of Mounted Police as in the old days, for instance, before 1906, when autonomy was granted to Saskatchewan and Alberta? It was thought then that we would not require as many mounted police after that as we had had before.

It is only right that the committee should have a statement showing the present position of the Mounted Police and their relation to the different provinces. I shall be glad to make such a statement after recess.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the Committee rose at six o'clock I promised the leader of the Opposition that I would make a statement with reference to the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and the relation of that Force to the Western Provinces. I had intended to speak on this particular aspect of the matter when we came to the next item, but probably it is just as well to give the information on this item relating to civil government, as any matter connected with the Force can properly be discussed under it.
As my hon. friend will recall, Parliament established t#e Force in 1873. Up to the creation of tihe Western Provinces tire Mounted Police had exercised police jurisdiction in Western Canada, other than British Columbia, and had been the only police force performing general police duty in that western land, When the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were formed,

agreements were entered into between the Federal Government and these Provincial Governments under which the Royal Northwest Mounted Police continued to perform police duties within these provinces-, the provinces paying a oer-tain annual subvention to the Federal Government in return for such services. That situation continued without change, the agreement being renewed from time to time until the autumn of 1916, when, owing to the conditions which had developed through the war, it was considered desirable by the Federal Government that the Mounted Police should be relieved from further ordinary police duties in the provinces. I should have added that the Mounted Police were performing certain police duties in Manitoba also under an agreement with the Government of that province. In the fall of 1916, as I say, the Federal Government came to the conclusion that it was in the public interest that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police should be relieved of further duties under these agreements with the Provincial Governments so that they might be free to devote themselves wholly to their duties under the Dominion authorities. One of the main reasons which led to that con-elusion was the situation which existed in the United States at that time, the country to the south not having, entered the war and a great deal of unrest existing there. Certain investigations had been conducted by the American police which showed a good deal of pro-German activity in certain sections of the United States. We had a large alien population in Western Canada, and it was deemed necessary *that the Mounted'Police should be free to carefully patrol *the international boundary and protect us against such proGerman activities; to supervise all matters connected with the administration of the law relating to aliens in Western Canada, and generally to exercise police supervision in those matters over, which the Federal Government had jurisdiction throughout the western provinces. Therefore on the 29th of November, 1916, after a -conference with each of the provincial governments, ari* understanding was arrived at, whereby the then existing agreements were terminated, and from that date the Royal Northwest Mounted Police have not been performing any police dutiel under any general agreement with the provincial governments. When the United States entered the war, the situation in reference to- pro-German activities in the
United States, and possible troubles in Canada arising therefrom, was completely changed, and the Royal Northwest Mounted Police expressed a desire to be allowed to serve overseas-in fact from the very outbreak of the war they had been desirous of going to the front as a unit, but owing to the view which the Government entertained as to the importance of maintaining a strong force in Western Canada, it did not feel free to grant their request. That request was renewed in 1917, and again in 1918. In the summer of 1917 an offer was made to the Imperial Government of a cavalry unit from the Mounted Police, but at that time the authorities in England did not desire such a unit. The offer was renewed in the following winter or the spring of 1918, with practically the same result. However, in the great German offensive of March and April, 1918, our Canadian cavalry brigade suffered very serious casualties, and in the month of April the Overseas Minister of Militia cabled out to Canada for a substantial number of cavalry reinforcements. Knowing that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police had been anxious to serve at the front as a cavalry regiment, the offer was made to them to provide the necessary reinforcements to be sent overseas to strengthen our cavalry brigade. Subsequently the plans were changed so as to provide reinforcements for the cavalry brigade, and at the same time furnish a squadron of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police to add to the existing corps cavalry. I am glad to say that when the announcement was made to the Police that they could volunteer for overseas service, notwithstanding the critical condition that then existed on the Western Front and the serious casualties that-our cavalry brigade had sustained, every man of military age in the force, and many not of military age, volunteered for service overseas. Only those that were physically fit could be taken, but although only some five hundred men were asked for we secured reinforcements at that time to the number of twelve officers and seven hundred and thirty-six of other ranks, including exmembers of the force and other volunteers, and they proceeded overseas on the 14th of June. The force completed their training at Shorncliffe, where I had the opportunity of inspecting them, and I have never seen a finer body of men. At Shorncliffe they divided, one squadron proceeding to France in the- month of October where they were first attached to the Canadian Light Horse. Subsequently they were at-

tached to and formed part of the corps cavalry, and acted as despatch riders and patrols for the several divisions. As soon as the armistice was signed a squadron was pushed over to Namur, Belgium, and one troop under I ieutenant Acland, was sent into Germany with the Army of Occupation. The others who formed the balance of the force that went overseas, were divided and seven non-commissioned officers and two hundred and thirty-six of other ranks were formed part of a tank unit for service in France. The balance of the original force were utilized as reinforcements for our cavalry brigade in .France.	The majority of those
that went overseas have already returned or are now returning. Major Jennings, who was in command of the unit, is, II believe, now on the ocean on his way back with some one hundred and seventy-five men, and when they have reached Canada the greater number of those who went overseas will have returned. *
While on this subject, let me add that, when, the Government decided to send certain troops to Siberia, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police was asked to provide a cavalry squadron. The request came on the ,17th of August, 1918. We immediately complied and the squadron was completely mobilized on the 9th September, consisting of six officers and one hundred and eighty-one of other ranks, and proceeded overseas to Siberia. As the members of the Committee are aware, those troops are now being returned from that country; a few of the Mounted Police are back, but the majority have not yet returned.
I mention these details in connection with the service overseas, because I think it is only fair to the force that one should point out how anxious they were to serve during the whole period of the war, and how quickly they responded when the opportunity was afforded them. Although those who went to France did not see much of the actual fighting, except as despatch riders, and serving in a similar capacity, it was not because they were not anxious to do so. In speaking of their services overseas, I think I should mention the fact that, while the Government was not able to let the force go over as a unit, large numbers of the Police resigned their positions, or purchased their discharge as they were entitled to do in order that they might proceed to Europe and serve at the front.
I am advised by the commissioner that during the period from the outbreak of the war up to the time we mobilized the seven or eight hundred men for service in France,
[M,r. Rowell.]
probably not less, than 1,000 men had resigned from the Northwest Mounted Police in order to serve overseas, and those men have won distinction on all the fields where they fought. I wish I had time to tell the House of some of the deeds of those gallant men. I will only mention two. The famous Michael O'Leary, V.O., was one of the Northwest Mounted Police, and he set a standard for courage and bravery during the early days of the war which many other gallant soldiers have since emulated. The other, a constable in the ranks for two-years-Constable Parkes, a young man now twenty-seven years of age. In 1915 he purchased his discharge to go to the front; he rose to the command of the 116th Battalion, C.E.F., and won the V. C., the D. S. O., and La Croix de Guerre. He proved himself an officer of the highest efficiency, and has been selected by the Canadian Corps to attend the staff college. I might mention other members of the force and the gallant service they have rendered, but time does not permit. I should also mention that ex-members of the force-that is men who had served in the force-provided our Canadian army overseas with two major-generals, four brigadier generals, and colonels, majors and captains by the score. It shows the type of men who are serving in our Royal Northwest Mounted Police. .All the sons, of military age, of the present and past officers have served overseas, and no less than ten officers' sons died on the battlefield. The son of the-first man who joined the force in 1873 is an hon. and gallant member of this House- Brigadier-General Griesbach,' who has rendered such distinguished service in this war. He is o*e of the many gall^pt officers' sons of members of the force who have served overseas.
Now, my hon. friend has asked about the relations of the force to the provinces, and what is the future of the force? The agreements with the provinces having expired, and the provinces having established their own police forces, and so large a percentage of the force having enlisted for overseas service, the question very naturally arose in the minds of the members of the force and of the people *of Western Canada : What is to be the future of the force? Has it served its purpose? Shall we let the provinces look after their own police duties and discontinue the force which has existed for so many years? One of the principal reasons why I visited Western Canada last year was to look into the situation on the ground in order to decide as to the future of the Northwest Mounted Police.

And I must say that wherever I went I found but one opinion-'the force should be continued, that it would be a calamity to discontinue this magnificent force, which rendered such conspicuous service to Western Canada ever since it was organized in 1873.
If it was to be continued what should be its future? There were two possible courses open:	Either that it should form the
nucleus of a permanent Federal police force for the Dominion; or that it should *constitute one of the cavalry units in our permanent military force. That was a question which we felt we were not in a position to decide at the time, and therefore we deemed it advisable to continue the force as a police force in the meantime, leaving the question of what its final character should be to be determined according to circumstances at a later date. But we did determine, and it was necessary we should determine in order to preserve the morale of the force, that the force should not be discontinued, but that the force with its splendid record should be preserved as a national asset for the Dominion.
We concluded that for the time being, at least, there were many important duties which a Federal mounted police force should continue to discharge, and that it was our duty to piaintain it for the performance of those duties. Therefore when my hon. friend asks about the relations of the provinces to the Northwest Mounted Police, I would say that this force at the present time does not take the place of >the provincial or municipal police in any of the provinces in the ordinary administration of the law. It does not supersede them; it supplements their work when required. But its primary duties are in connection with the enforcement of legislation in which the Federal Government is particularly interested. It will appear in the Estimates -the next item to which I referred in opening-that we are proposing that the force should be recruited up to the full authorized strength of 1,200. As the force was only some 600 strong -last year, I only presented estimates for its then existing strength, and as it has been decided to recruit it up to the full authorized strength, the estimates this year are necessarily correspondingly increased.
For some time past the force has been responsible for the enforcement of the Military Service Act; and the various Acts in reference to aliens; the policing of the Dominion Government parks-that is done under an arrangement with the provincial governments, whereby the force looks after
the whole police work in those parks;-it is performing certain duties for the Department of Immigration in administering the immigration laws'; in fact, it has, throughout the war been performing very important duties in seeing that men of undesirable character should not cross the international boundary contrary to the provisions of the immigration laws. It is also performing certain important duties in connection with the Department of Indian Affairs ; it is looking after the patrol of the international boundary and the enforcement of the customs laws; it is also looking after the enforcement of the inland revenue laws in these Western Provinces-all matters in which the Federal Government is particularly interested ; and in addition it provides an important force, available at the call of the provincial governments, for the maintenance of law and order throughout those western territories. In addition it has important duties to perform in the Northwest Territories which I shall mention in a minute or two. I should add that when we decided to continue the force we also decided to extend its jurisdiction to [DOT] British Columbia and to certain portions of Ontario. It will come to the easterly limit of Military District No. 10, the headquarters of which is in the city of Winnipeg. _ The distribution of the proposed force of 1,200 men is as follows:-

Let me say a word or two with reference to the Northwest Territories. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police is the only police force looking after the administration of justice and the preservation of law and order in the Northwest Territories, and it has similar duties in the Yukon. Probably there is nothing finer in the whole history of the force than the work it is doing in those extreme northern portions of the continent. There are three posts within the Arctic circle, Herschell Island, in the Arctic ocean, Fort McPherson and Barnard Harbour, which is right on the Arctic ocean. When the report of the Mounted Police for this year is printed and particularly when the Supplementary Report which gives an account of the Baker Lake patrol is printed, I hope the members of the House will read both these documents, because the

latter records one of the finest incidents in the -whole history of the force. I stop to mention it because it is just such a fine example of courage and achievement as is disclosed in that report which gives the Eoyal Northwest Mounted Police its splendid reputation and which makes it such a powerful factor in -the preservation of law and order. It shows the respect which the people of the country have for the men who compose the force and it illustrates the manner in which law is enforced and justice administered under the British Crown.
In 1913, two American explorers, Messrs. Street and Radford were murdered by some Eskimo tribes at Bathurst inlet on the Arctic ocean, and this was reported to the Mounted Police. It became their duty to endeavour to hunt up the murderers. It was not possible to send the Mounted Police in 1913 as we had none in that district in 1913. A patrol had to be carefully organized and properly equipped, and that was done in 1914. This patrol set out from Halifax on July 31, 1914, for Chesterfield Inlet on the Northwest side of Hudson's .Bay. The intention was to establish a base at the east end of Baker lake lying west of Chesterfield Inlet, buit owing to adverse weather conditions it was not possible to reach Baker lake in 1914 and so the expedition proceeded to Port Nelson. In 1915 the base was established at Baker Lake and during the winter 1915-16 threw out an advance depot on Thelon river. They had to put in caches ahead to provide provisions and supplies. In 1917 Inspector French took charge and the patrol set out in March, Sergeant-Major Caulkin accompanying Inspector French. They travelled, to go in, 2,483 miles and almost a corresponding distance to come out, the total patrol being not less than 4,500 miles over a territory hitherto untrodden by white men, with the possible exception of one explorer. They had to carry a certain amount of provisions, and for the rest they had to depend upon shooting musk ox and other animals of the country. On their way out their provisions were exhausted; their dogs were impoverished, and they had to keep some of their dogs alive by killing the others and feeding the meat to the dogs. Inspector French and his companions were compelled for three days to live on soup made partially by boiling their moccasins, and then they had to tramp on hour after hour in order to reach their goal. They reached their objective; they made the investigation; they ascertained the facts; they brought fiMr. Rowell.]
back and -presented a full and complete report. It is such courage and devotion to duty _upon the part of our Northwest Mounted Police that give them their unique place in the hearts and affections of the people of Western Canada-a place that nothing can imperil or destroy.
Let me mention one other incident before I leave this point. An Eskimo woman was murdered at Bathurst inlet, and the report of this murder reached the Mounted Police in 1917. One Mounted Policeman, -Corporal Conway, started out in August, 1917, to travel across country into the Arctic circle to endeavour to locate the murderers. That one Mounted Policeman went into the Arctic circle, hunted up the murderers and he arrested them though he was surrounded by hostile Eskimo, and brought them out, and they were tried at Fort McPherson in December, 1918. He was absent from August, 1917 to December, 1918, in those Arctic wilds-one man amongst all the Eskimo people. This shows the respect in which the .Mounted Police are held by all people in that north country. The people know that if a crime is committed, the Mounted Police will hunt at out, follow up the criminal, and that those who are guilty will be punished. It is because we have such a splendid force so valuable for the preservation of law and order that the Dominion Government has decided for the time being that the force should be maintained to the full authorized strength of 1,200 men, for the purposes I have mentioned

I am sure all the Western members and, indeed, all members, -were pleased to hear the tribute paid to the Royal Northwest Mounted Police- by the President of the Privy Council. The service rendered by that force is well known throughout Canada. The minister men tioned, amongst other things, that the first Victoria Cross gained during this great war was gained by a member or an ex-membei of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. The first Victoria Cross thaj was granted in the South African War went also to a member of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, namely, Sergeant A. H. Richardson. I am pleased to note that the minister appreciates this fact because he is in a position to do something to remedy a grievance of long standing which I am not going to mention, but which was given into the hands of an hon. member on the other side, and which, I have no doubt, will be brought up this evening. We are all glad to know that the force instead of being decreased is

to be increased and brought up to full strength. That is right. For the few years during which they were not actively engaged, the law of the country was no*- as well administered and every one felt the effect thereof. The minister, in telling what the intention of the Government was, failed to tell us what is the pay received by the men, non-commissioned officers and officers. That would be of interest, because we in this House might then judge whether they were getting adequate pay for the services rendered.
The pay was increased last autumn by fifty cents per day to all the constables and non-commissioned officers of the force.

What is the total
pay?
A junior constable starts in at $1.50 a day. A married man gets double rations, which would be equivalent to about $3 a day.

I must say that for the services rendered the pay does not seem to be very large, and it must be very difficult for the members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police to raise a family on that wage, especially when we consider that labourers to-day are striking for $3.50 to $4 a day. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police under the present Administration-I do not know the reason, and I am not going to criticise at the moment-find it harder to get along to-day than they did a few years ago. Perhaps the minister will tell the House why a change in policy was made, as a result of which the men are to-day centered at headquarters in the large cities, where the cost of living is so much greater, irfstead of being distributed throughout the country as they, were formerly. Travelling on 'the trains I meet a great many of these boys, and the complaint I hear is that it is almost impossible for them to live. If the reason for the change in policy is that more efficient service can be rendered by the men being centered in the large cities, the reason is a good one, but I cannot understand the change being made for any other reason, and it undoubtedly causes great hardship to the men. I am told that part of their duty in the city of Edmonton is to exercise their horses. In my time in the Mounted Police the trouble was to make our horses last; we sometimes used to have spare horses. The Government has mentioned some of the duties of the Mounted Police in connection with inland revenue and looking after alien enemies. Under the
present system the Government is put to the extra expense of sending the men, per* haps, a hundred miles down the line to where their services may be needed, and livery or automobiles have ^to be engaged to take them to their place of duty. Under the old system that expense was avoided, and the men could get to where they were required very much quicker when the call for their services came. They would have their horses right there and could render quicker and better service. There was also the advantage I have mentioned of cheaper living in the. small towns. I really cannot understand how a married man, even with double rations, can live in the city of Edmonton on $1.50 a day. It does not seem to be fair, considering the cost of living, and the services these men are rendering the country, and the minister himself has told us what really splendid service it is. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police should be dealt with a little more generously, and it should be made as easy as possible for them to live and bring up a family. Rent in Edmonton to-day is very high, and the cost of living is just as high as in the city of Ottawa. I repeat, I really cannot see how these men can bring up their families on such a wage. I do not think there would be the least objection throughout the country; indeed, I think it would only be fair to the men who are giving such splendid service if the pay started at $2 or $2.50, with the regular good-conduct pay after that,
