speechtext:
Before this discussion goes any further, I must draw the attention of the Committee to the fact that the item under consideraion is No. 11, which relates only to salaries here at the head office. The discussion has been very interesting, and J do not want to interrupt it any way, but 1 think we should either pass the item now under consideration, or hold this discussion over until we consider item 254, which provides for tihe pay of the force, subsistence, billeting, etc.
Northwest Territories, Yukon Territory, Province of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia and part of Western Ontario-Pay of force, $1,007,984.90-Subsistence, billeting, forage and dog feed, fuel and light, clothing, repairs and renewals, horses, arms and ammunition, stationery, medical stores, transport, water service, building repairs and contingencies, $1,230,520.18-To compensate members of the Royal Nortwest Mounted Police for injuries received while in the discharge of duty, $5,000- $2,24'9,5'05.08.

It has been my pleasure for some thirty-two years to live within

two miles of the headquarters of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and during that period I have had the pleasure of following very closely the work that has been done by this excellent body of men. I have been able to see how their administration of the law was accepted by the people of that part of the country, and I fully agree with the President of the Privy Council that when it was decided a few years ago to discontinue the services of the force, the people of Western Canada objected very much. Wherever I heard the people discussing the matter, and I did hear them very often, invariably they expressed exceeding regret that they were to lose the services of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. It was fully recognized by our people that the provinces had the right to administer the law, and that they were within their rights in asserting themselves, but notwithstanding that, our people did not want to lose the Royal Northwest Mounted Police because they knew that the "red coat" as he was familiarly known carried with him a prestige which no provincial body of men, no matter how good they might be or how free from political influence, could possibly build up for many years to come. After watching this force all these years and seeing what the result of their enforcement of the law has been, I have no hesitation in saying that their administration of the law in the Northwest Territories, and subsequently in the provinces for a period of several years, was the sanest administration of the law that this world has ever seen. A police force can create trouble just about as easily as it can allay it. If given to irritating methods in their administration of the law, to spying or resorting to trickery, or "stool pigeons," or anything of that kind, a police force can in a very short time stir 'up an animosity which will do more harm than can be outweighed by any good that they may do. But no such administration was known under the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. As a matter of fact, ever since I first knew the force it has been composed entirely of picked men; men of low type were not accepted. After the men had been picked and taken in the force, they received a training not only in the law itself, but in the administration of the law, which made it possible for them to give that administration which has been so acceptable to the people of that part of the country. It is not necessary to multiply instances in 
proof of the fact that in the opinion of the people of Western Canada the Royal Northwest Mounted Police has no superior. Such being the case, we are exceedingly desirous that the force shall be continued in our country, and we were just as pleased to learn a year or so ago that the force was to be re-established as we had been regretful to hear some time previously that it was to be disbanded. To-day we are told that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police are to be given practically new duties- naturally their duties will not be the same as they were before, for now we have provincial police forces in all the provinces which will have their own jurisdiction. These new duties will absorb a great deal of the time and attention of the Mounted Police, and will require a very strong force. Among other things, we are told, they are to administer the law made by this Parliament in regard to aliens. I suppose somebody will at once say that probably that means that our alien population in Western Canada requires severe policing. Such is not the case. I know whereof I speak, for I have no less an authority than Commissioner Perry himself,-and he can contradict me any time he sees fit, for he is not very far away-when I say that since the outbreak of the war our alien population in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta (and we have over 300,000 aliens in Saskatchewan) have not given us any trouble at all. There has been no rioting, and they have caused no disturbance. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police have so sanely administered the law and have dealt with them in such a just and generous manner that they have never felt in any way called upon to resort to violence. The aliens today, at any rate wherever I have met them, have shown that they know that the 'Royal Northwest Mounted Police will not tolerate any nonsense. They recognize that the police will administer the law with a smile and will not resort to trickery or anything of that kind, and that they will give to the aliens exactly the same protection as is afforded other people, all that is expected oF them being that they shall respect the law. The aliens in that part of the country to-day are just as willing and anxious as any one else to have the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, for they know that they will be given protection as long as they obey the law. That is exactly the conditions that we -want to see prevailing in Western Canada. We do not want any aliens to feel that they have to be kept there by force; they must be mdde to realize that

the law is their law, as much for their protection as for that of any other citizens. I doubt very much if there is any other police body that could deal with these aliens at the present time as can the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. There is, it must be admitted, some excitement in Canada today, and a certain amount of ill-feeling on the part of a portion of the population towards some aliens, and it would not do to choose any number of policemen from amongst that type of men to enforce the law against these aliens or to deal with them in any shape or form, because if we do so we shall create instead of allaying trouble. On the other hand, the Mounted Police, from their experience in dealing with this class of people, can go amongst them, as they have done for years and years, and so conduct matters as to give us law and order without any clash at all. We do not want clash between any two sets of people, and I am satisfied that the Royal Mounted Police can effect that condition better than any other body. The matter of pay was referred to by the hon. member for Victoria, Alberta (Mr. White), who, I believe, was himself a member of the Royal Mounted Police, and whom we are pleased to recognize as such. As far as pay is concerned, I believe that the men are not getting sufficient. Indeed, for many years they have not been getting enough, and I do not believe they were ever paid an adequate salary. We should remember that these are picked men, who have the ability to command high pay in any walk of life, and men of their type should not be asked to serve the country for lower pay than they can get elsewhere. I therefore support the suggestion that their pay be made such as will retain to our country the services of men who have had experience and training and know precisely how to handle the situation as it exists to-day. I sincerely hope that in this new arrangement the Government will see fit to make use of the large body of men who have served in the Mounted Police and who are now following other occupations. There is a great reserve body which can be made use of in the capacity that is required, and I hope the Government will take them into consideration in this new arrangement, and adapt their policy to that end.

I did not hear all the minister had to say, but the portion of his remarks that I did hear I very gladly endorse, especially his eulogies of this splendid body of men and his view's in regard to their excellent record. I shall not discuss
the points raised by the other speakers regarding higher pay and other matters connected with the force at present. I wish, however, to bring to the attention of the House a matter which I believe should be considered by the Government, and I think that if there is a favourable expression of opinion by the House to-night, the ./Government will perhaps be inclined to give it consideration.
It is a matter of long standing and perhaps may be considered somewhat out of date, but in view of the very eulogistic terms in which the minister spoke of the service and the record of this force, I think this is an opportune time to look back for a few years and consider whether we have dealt justly with these men in the past. To quote the minister's words, they have a splendid reputation and record, and, added the minister, there have seldom been such exhibitions of courage and heroism as we see constantly manifested throughout the years by this splendid force. Indeed, this is a matter of history, and with these sentiments the people of the country generally are in accord, especially those who have lived in the West for a great many years, who have learned not only to respect and honour these men, but to admire them in the highest degree. The force has been particularly fortunate in the splendid leaders it has had in the past, and the sanity of its administration has been largely due to that leadership and the discipline and excellent record of the men individually. At the time of the Northwest Rebellion, I suppose that of all the forces engaged in that rebellion the Royal Northwest Mounted Police can very properly be accorded one of the highest places, if not the highest place. These men gave their services at that time, and although it is true they were simply doing their plain duty, they did splendid work. After the rebellion was over the militia and other forces were [DOT]granted scrip in recognition of their services. lit was, not very valuable, but still it was a recognition. They were given a medal and scrip and for many years the Northwest Mounted Police were unable even to get the medal in recognition of their splendid services during that rebellion. I cannot understand why there should have been the delay there was, but after a great many years, and after the matter had been brought to the attention of the successive *Governments of the times during which it was in abeyance, a medal was finally granted to them, but no scrip was ever given to the veterans of the Northwest Mounted Police. This matter has been dealt



with at various times without success, and I am going to take the liberty, with the indulgence of the Committee, of reading a letter placed in my hands and a resolution by the Royal Northwest (Mounted Police Veterans' Association. This association numbers about 400 members who have served in this splendid body and have retired. A great many of them are now well on in years, having spent most of their life in the police service, and some of them are none too well off. The letter is as follows:
Royal North-West Mounted Police Veterans' Association.
Sir,-At a meeting of the RJN.W.M. Police Veterans' Association held on the 25th day of March last, the matter of long-standing injustice to those members of the force who served during the Riel Rebellion in the year 1885 was discussed'.
For several years after the rebellion both the medal and the land scrip were withheld from the members of this force, but' both the medal and, scrip were issued to other units, both regulars (A and B battery) and! volunteers, taking part. After years of long and continued insistence, the medals were issued to members of this force 'but not the land scrip, Why the discrimination in favour of other bodies taking part in the rebellion, against the (North-West Mounted Police has never been explained. That the N.W.M. Police did their duty equally with the other units engaged, was in a measure acknowledged (though late) by the issue of the medal, therefore if it be admitted that the medal was rightly issued, why is the scrip withheld?
Therefore, it is unanimously resolved:- " That this Association one more petition the Government of Canada to do justice to those members of the R.N.W.M. Police who took part in the Rebellion, that the scrip be issued, thereby removing the stigma and injustice to those who gave their loyal and faithful service. That the Government be reminded that members of this force, have, on many occasions since, performed valuable service to this country, and more especially have many of them brought honour to Canada in the South African War and in the last great war, also that the members who took part in the 18'8'5 rebellion, and who we strongly belileve are entitled to the land scrip, are now getting up in years, and the issue of the scrip at this time, would enable many of them to end their [DOT]days with some degree of comfort, together with the satisfaction of the knowledge of the recognition of their loyal and faithful service for the Dominion of Canada and Empire."
C. R. Filtness, Secy.
In answer to that itr has been stated and argued that this matter has been considered by the governments of Sir John Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden, and that the present Government feel that the decision arrived at by previous governments should be sustained. That decision was that inasmuch as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police were simply doing their duty in putting down the rebellion, they were not entitled to this scrip, flMr. Stevens.]
that they were not on a parity with the volunteers and that the scrip was for volunteers only. In answer to that contention, there are certain arguments which I think I should bring to the attention of the House. You will note that I referred to the fact that A and B Batteries which, I think came from Kingston, were engaged. They were regular soldiers doing their duty in exactly the same way as the Mounted Police. Yet A and B Batteries received the privilege of taking land scrip just the same as the militia units. I do not wish to suggest that there was any prejudice but I must confess that, after looking through this matter with a considerable degree of care, I am inclined to think that perhaps at the time of the rebellion, and shortly afterwards, there was indeed some slight degree of prejudice against the men of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and that the militia units, and the commanders of the militia units, may have considered that their special duty was to look after the volunteer forces and not the regulars, that the Mounted Police should take care of themselves in any case, being regular soldiers, and that therefore they did not merit any special attention. I do not look at the matter in that light at all.
It seems that this is a very opportune time to consider the case of the members of this force in view of the statement made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) to the effect that there is some difficulty in retaining the services of some of the most efficient men by reason of the fact that the encouragement is very slight and is probably not isufflcient. I am not going to discuss that but I will say that the men of this gallant force, at the conclusion of a certain period of service, should be entitled to recognition, whether land scrip or something else, that would be an encouragement for them.
There is no body of men in existence to-day, nor has there been in all history, even taking the illustration given by the minister himself, which hap performed such valiant service in opening up to the world that new country. We may talk about explorers and about the records of the members of the geological survey and other survey parties, but these pioneers who, in performance of their duty, launched forth into the wilderness away up into the Arctic circle, and who were often away from civilization for two or three years at a time, learned to know all about those regions, and from them and from
9 p.m. the very minute and intelligent reports they gave to their officers

and to the department, we know a great deal about the hinterland of Canada. Unquestionably, many of these men would gladly settle in some region where they have spent the greater portion of their lives as civilization and city life have little attraction for them. But we give them absolutely no encouragement. We give them the small pay of the regular force. I do not know that they have complained very much about that, but why should not we not only recognize the services of these men in the Northwest Rebellion of 1885, hut also give a gratuity of some kind to which the members of the force might look forward?
Another point I have to make is this: It is not a very important point, but I am led to make it because apparently it is necessary to make every possible argument in favour of these men to enable them to get any consideration at all. It was argued that these men were not on the same basis as the volunteers. The answer to that is that they were under the command of the volunteer militia of Canada. You may say that is quibbling, you may say it is too fine an argument, but if you are going to tell these men that they are not going to receive this gratuity because they are simply regulars, I answer that I will quibble as well, if you like to call it that, and I will say that at that time they were under exactly the same commanders as the militia force of Canada and in my judgment one argument has equal force with the other.
It is also stated that there was too great a delay, that the matter should have been brought to the notice of the Government before. It has been brought to the attention of the House on many occasions. It has been brought to the attention of the Government over and over again from the time of Sir John Macdonald upwards. But there is a reason for that delay in recent years, and it is that many members of the police force serving in 1885 remained on the strength of the force for a certain time and during that time it would have been a serious breach of discipline on the part of the members to urge their claim for land scrip. That is obvious. That is not a narrow or stringent argument, it is a fair statement of the case. We know that these men have been under the strictest discipline. None know better than the Government or the Government officials that had these men, while they were still members of the force, brought any particular pressure to bear upon the Government to induce them to grant this scrip, they would have been
148i
very severely disciplined for doing so, and, it may be wisely so-that is a point that I am not disputing. Now that they are out of the force, after long years of service, they have, like other bodies, grouped themselves together in this Veterans' Association, and they come to the Government and say: Now, give us justice.
Sir, I consider that a grave injustice has been done these men, not only in not giving them their medals after so many years' service, but in not giving them this scrip. It may be argued that it is late, but that is no argument or real reason why we should hesitate to make good the discrepancy now. I think if it is recognized, and I am sure the Committee will be prompt to recognize it, that an injustice has been perpetrated in this case, we should agree at once that the injustice should be remedied forthwith. There is another reason why delay has occurred. The question was raised in 1913, but shortly after that the war broke out, and it was not desirable to press the matter while hostilities were in progress. That is perfectly clear. This House was occupied during almost the last five years in the consideration of the most momentous questions. To have brought this matter up during that period would have looked rather trifling, and therefore it was not brought forward. Now that the war is over, and we are able to give some sort of cleaning to the slate, as it were, I think we might very well clean this matter off. The feeling has arisen in the minds of these men that they have been discriminated against, and I must confess that after talking to a large number of them, and finding them not only intelligent, but intensely loyal and splendid fellows in every respect, I was impressed with the fact that they were suffering under discrimination, that there was no fair, logical reason that could be advanced why they should not have received this scrip lopg ago, and I see no fair, logical reason why it should not be given them to-day. There is no argument so far as I can see, that can be advanced against doing what is requested here, except that it is not wanted to be done. Now, Sir, I put it to the minister personally, and as strongly as I can, that he recognize the courage and the heroism of these men, that he recognize the services that they have performed in the past by admitting their just claim-a claim unanimously advanced by this association, numbering about four hundred; not a very large number, in fact a comparatively small one-and give to them the privilege of taking up scrip somewhere in the Government lands in the West, just as

the Militia Force of Canada at that time were rewarded with scrip. I am not going to argue as to the type of scrip to be granted; I do not care, nor do they, what reasonable restrictions are imposed. In any case, give to these men in the closing years of life, the satisfaction of knowing that they have at last been fully recognized, and remove from their minds all thought or suspicion that the country does not recognize that they have w'ell performed their duty.

This is probably one of the most important items in the expenditure affecting Canada, more particularly the Western Provinces, although the amount involved is not large. I agree with all the words of praise which have been uttered on behalf of the Eoyal Northwest Mounted Police, and if every member in this House to-night were to utter similar praise I do not believe that we would overstate the case on behalf of these valiant men. They have rendered a service to Western Canada which could not have been performed by any other body of men; and the difference between the pioneer days in our country beyond the Great Lakes, and those in the Western States-a difference in which Canada compares very favourably with the pioneer period of any other country in the world-is due to the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and the traditions which have been established in connection with that magnificent body of men. The red tunics of the police as they rode over the plains of the West created an impression upon the minds of the man who came in there, whether as a genuine settler or as an outlaw, that the affairs of this Dominion were administered in accordance with the principles of law and on the basis of justice and equity for all. It was impossible in those early days for any mischievous doctrines such as now appear to be in order to make any headway in that Western country, and I am very glad that the Government has seen fit to re-establish this fine force in connection with the administration of law in the West. I must confess that I was somewhat surprised when I heard the minister announce that the force was to be increased to the extent of only twelve hundred men, and that it was to exercise jurisdiction over the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territory, the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, and part of Western Ontario. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if the force had been increased to

some three thousand men instead of twelve hundred, the Government would not be providing any stronger force than is necessary to administer law in Western Canada. We might just as well face the facta as they exist. We know that the conditions that prevail throughout the civilized world-whether it be in Europe, or in Great Britain, or in the United States, or in Canada-are vastly different from those which previously existed at any time in the world's history. We know that in the past days men have gone through Canadian cities preaching their doctrines from soap boxes at street corners, and little heed or attention was paid to them. We know throughout the United States and throughout Canada at the present time, however, there are many disciples of anarchy, and men who are advocating secretly, and in some cases openly, the subversion of law and order by means of physical force. We cannot close our eyes to this serious condition, and it is the duty of this Government to establish a body of police to so administer our law that any man who comes from a land where they have trampled the government under foot and resisted all law shall be taught that he cannot come and preach that doctrine in Canada with impunity, but must be bound by the law and observe order here. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that if there is any fault to be found with this Government in connection with that question, it is that it has not taken the reins of justice in its hands as firmly as it should have done. I believe the Government has been too lenient with a certain class of people who are going throughout the country sowing the seed of anarchy and destruction. The men to whom I allude urge the overthrow of the Government not by means of argument or reason, or process of evolution; they advocate that all governments in the world shall be overthrown by physical force and violence. It is the duty of the force, to whose maintenance we are voting money to-night to go throughout the length and breadth of the territory confined to their care and where they find men-I care not whether they come from Germany, or Russia, or Austria, or any other country- who preach the doctrine that the Government of Canada should be overthrown by violence and force, and that the laws on our statute books should be resisted by physical force, they should gather those men in and ship them back to the country where such principles are in force.

The Northwest Mounted Police may have had a great work on their hands in pioneer days, but I believe that they have a far greater work on their hands at the present time. As has been pointed out by the member for Regina, they have succeeded in enforcing observance of the law and commanding order in this country, not by violence themselves, but by the great care and tact they have shown in the performance of their duties. We want that same class of man now to exercise those same qualities, to uphold the dignity of the law as they upheld it in the pioneer days of the west, and if they do that they will render the greatest service to this country that can possibly be rendered by any police body.	'	'
Now, if we ask 1,200 men to perform those duties, are we not placing upon them a greater burden than they can bear and perform their duties efficiently? Their jurisdiction wiE extend from the remote parts of the Yukon Territory to the remote parts of western Ontario-1,200 men scatr tered over that vast area. I submit that their duties cannot be performed with justice to this country. I submit, Mr. Chairman, through you to the Minister that he should reconsider his decision to increase this body to 1,200 men, and should have anywhere from three to five thousand men. It might involve an expenditure of $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 instead of $2,000,000 or $3,000,000. But would it not be better to spend that larger sum and rid our country of men who are a menace, men who are the opponents of law and order and justice? Would we not save much for the future? I care not about any man in this country who may hold views of government which are different from those held by the majority. Any man has the right to perfect freedom of speech, he can argue for any form of government he pleases as long as he proceeds by constitutional methods to arrive at that destination; but the line of demarcation is between that class of men-who are welcome in this country-and the class who come here or who are living here and who say: We know no law, we know no government; we are going to upset governments, we are going to resist laws by the utmost physical force and by the violence which we command. We do not want that class.
I want to point out to the Government that when the Northwest Mounted Police have come in contact with those men, and meted out speedy justice to them, as they must, their hands must be upheld, there
must be no political interference, there must be no sympathy shown, the law must be supreme and they should be backed to the limit. We want to rid our country of lawless agitators, and the sooner we put this machinery in operation and rid ourselves of that revolutionary element the better for the Dominion of Canada and the better for her lawful citizens.

It seems almost superfluous after all the praise that has been lavished upon the Northwest Mounted Police for any one to add to that praise. However, the speakers who have preceded me are all from the Western Provinces, Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and as the jurisdiction of the force is to be extended to the head of the lakes, I wish to commend the Government for having reached that decision.
I have heard nothing but praise of that action, for the reason that every one in Western Ontario is glad to have a body of such noble traditions placed in charge of the enforcement of law and order in their territory. I have heard on one or two occasions very slight criticism, but it was from those who thought perhaps law and order should not be preserved.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) has advocated strengthening the Northwest Mounted Police Force for the purpose of preserving law and order. I believe the Government has studied very carefully the possibilities of strengthening the Force and I thoroughly agree that they should at least be recruited up to 1,200 men as is proposed. If the strengthening of the Force is for the purpose of keeping down Bolshevism and revolution in this country,
I believe the Government is well advised in the course it has taken. No one wishes this country to get in the chaotic condition which has overtaken Russia. Bolshevism means lawlessness, it means hunger and starvation, it means disruption, and we do not wish those conditions to extend to Canada.
I would like, if one might suggest to the Government what has been suggested to them a number of times recently by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), that they do something more than they have already done-and I know they have deeply considered the subject-regarding the control of the high cost of living. I hope this is not out of order, Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as I believe that the two things go together: the strengthening of the Northwest Mounted Police, and the control as far as possible of the high cost of living, for the reason that

Bolshevism is simply another name for revolution; and hunger is the legitimate mother of revolution. People do not revolt when they are -happy, contented and well fed; they revolt when the high cost of living is beyond their reach-and to-day in this country the cost of living is beyond the reach of a great many people, perhaps not to the extent of starvation, but to the extent of forcing them to deny themselves many of those things that they had previously considered to be the necessaries of life.
The reason I mention this matter is that I hold in my hand a letter from Mr. R. J. McFall to the City Clerk of Fort William bearing on this question. He takes up a number of cases-I will not read the letter- of violations of the law by the cold storage warehouses in the neighbourhood. He names four cold storage warehouses, and he gives instances of violations of the law, totalling altogether 40, in regard to selling the necessaries of life to the people of this country, in other words, meat and eggs. To my mind, one of the reasons- why we should extend the power of the Northwest Mounted Police is because the high cost of living is due to the profiteering of such corporations, and that is why I wish to put this matter before the House. It possibly is stretching the order point a little in bringing it in here-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very sorry, but it is stretching it altogether too far. The hon. gentleman cannot be allowed to do so.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. But I still adhere to the point, without going further in discussing it, that two things are equally necessary-that the control of the high cost of living is as necessary as the expansion of the powers of the Northwest Mounted Police. I regret, Mr. Chairman, that you find it necessary to stop me proceeding with these details, because I think they would be interesting not only to the House and to you personally, but probably to the country at large. However, perhaps on another occasion I shall have an opportunity of dealing with the subject; but at least now I can go as far as to suggest that the Government should do everything -possible to control the high cost of living.
I wish to say that I support very strongly the proposal to strengthen the Northwest Mounted Police up to at least 1,200 men.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I differ with my friend (Mr. Manion) from the sister city in asking that the Force be increased only to 1,200 men. Their jurisdiction is to be extended to the

head of the lakes, and we know what their services are. In the past, some of us have had business relations with them, not in being arrested, but in carrying out the work which they have initiated. The policy of the Government is, I understand, to recruit up to the full strength of 1,200 men, but that is too small a number, judging from the number of foreign people in the large cities of the West. As the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) said, the force ought to be increased to probably 5,000 as a permanent force. We have some rather dangerous days ahead of us; there are in this country places to-day where there are hotbeds breeding a possible revolution, and the best force to meet that is the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. We have altogether too few of them in Canada.
I would ask the minister to take into serious consideration some recognition of members of the force who went overseas for the time they were away. I made a promise to a carload of them about the first year of the war. I noticed about as fine a lot of men in "civies" as one would want to see anywhere coming down on the train, and wondered who they were. I went forward and sat in the car with them and found out that they were Northwest Mounted policemen, going back to serve in the Imperial forces, many of them being reservists. While I chatted with them they urged one thing upon me, and I promised that if I ever had an opportunity I would bring it forward, namely, that as they were giving up a dollar a day pay to go overseas to serve and draw one shilling a day in England, if they came back to this country, Canada should, in some way, give them a little nest egg or stake to induce them to return, so that they would have something to settle down on and marry and become citizens of this country. The proposition seemed so reasonable that I promised to do what I could. I wrote the commissioner about the matter at the time and got his reply, the only reply he could give, namely, that Parliament had made no such provision. It is not yet settled that these Northwest Mounted policemen who have gone over and served in the Imperial forces will receive the six months' pay that our Canadian soldiers are getting. It is true they will get the six months' pay or bonus from the Imperial forces, but that will amount to only about $120, whereas if they had enlisted with the Canadian troops they would receive a bonus

of six months' pay of $500 or $600.
I understand there is difficulty in getting men of the right sort, and where can better men be obtained than amongst those who have had experience, and who have served overseas? Why not urge those men to come back and say to them: If you come back, not only will you be reinstated and your time count for the whole period you have been away, but the difference between the dollar a day you were receiving and the one shilling, or two shillings as it was afterwards increased to, will be paid to you? That will show our appreciation. Canada did that with some of her civil servants in the first part of the war, and why should we not do it with the very best civil servants we have? Vie should let those men know in every way we possibly can that we appreciate their services. We have possibly dark days ahead of us, and we have two police forces in Canada, one the Northwest Mounted Police, and the other the Dominion Police. They are not members of any union; the Government have not the trouble with them that the city of Montreal or Toronto and other places have with their police force; they are loyal to the country, and any reasonable demand that they make should receive most careful consideration. They cannot urge their grievances as strongly as others can. For instance, there is the question of the bonus which is given to the Civil Service. It is a little out of order, but if the Dominion Police have a request regarding that, it should be most generously met, and we should not wait too long, until we turn their sympathies against us. I merely ask the minister if he will take into his most serious consideration the question of doing something for those men who were on the force, who enlisted and went overseas to serve in British regiments. I had a letter from Curragh camp a year after I had travelled with those boys, and the writer said; " Do you remember the fellow you were talking to in the train along the north shore of lake Superior? Here I am stuck at Curragh camp because they know that I am experienced in training men. Do you remember that freckled-faced boy with the green hat and the blue suit of clothes? That was Micky O'Leary who got the V.C. I wish I could get over and get the V.C. too. That is the type of men we should get back into the force. I urge strongly upon the minister not only to increase the force, but to bring back all the men who went overseas to serve with the colours.

With reference to the observations of various members, I should
first like to say a word or two regarding the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who has brought to the attention of the Committee the question of granting scrip to the members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police who served in the Rebellion of 1885. It is only right that I should give the Committee the' position of the matter as disclosed in the records of the House at that time. At the time when the rebellion occurred Sir John A. Macdonald, who was the minister responsible for the establishment of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, was, I believe, the minister in charge of the administration of the force. The reason why the Mounted Police were not granted the scrip appears to be that stated by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, namely, that the then Government looked upon their service as being rendered in the performance of duty, as they were responsible for the administration of law, and the preservation of order in the Northwest at that, time, and that the citizen soldiers who left their homes in other parts of Canada and went to the Northwest to put down the rebellion were in a different position. That is the ground upon which the then Prime Minister put the case for granting scrip to the volunteers. This is his statement as it appears in Hansard of 1885, page 3376;
We all agree that the services of our citizen soldiery, who have left their homes and their hearths in order to fight the battles of the country in the Northwest, and to restore peace, order and law, where disorder and insurrection existed, should be duly acknowledged. These resolutions are offered with that purpose, and they are offered with the secondary purpose of opening up that country for the young men of that soldiery, who have seen the Northwest, who know its advantages, and who may, perhaps, take a liking to the country and desire to settle there. It is of great importance too, I think, to tjhat country, and to the whole Dominion, that a considerable portion of that body should take up their habitation in the Northwest to which they have gone as loyal soldiers and as supporters of the supremacy of the law and of the Government of Canada, as, it is constituted.
The then Prime Minister went on to say that it was more than probable that a good portion of the militia force then on duty in the Northwest, would not desire to settle there, hut might return to their homes,_ and yet the Government should take recognition of their valuable services. Every one who settled there had the same right as any other settler to 160 acres of land. What was. then proposed was to give a second adjoining homestead of 160 acres, or 320 acres in all, instead of the usual 160 acres, and that they should receive their patent free of all charges. Those who return**

home and did not become settlers, would get scrip for 80 acres as an acknowledgment of their services. In concluding his explanation Sir John A. Macdonald said:
The resolutions have a two-fold object. First, that there should be a substantial recognition, beyond the mere daily pay of the militia men who went to the Northwest to fight our battles, of their services, by making them grants of land, or scrip if they don't want to have the land, and at the same time making a distinction between the men who will not settle there and the men who will. The man who does not, and who returns home, gets scrip equivalent to 80 acres; the man who goes there and settles there gets 320 acres.
In 1885 the militia men who were engaged in putting down the rebellion were awarded a medal. Under date of July 10, 1886, the medal was given to the Mounted Police, who were " actually under fire during the said troubles."
At different times the Northwest Assembly passed resolutions asking that the Mounted Police and the volunteers attached to the force be treated the same as the active militia as far as medals and scrip were concerned. In reply to the resolution of the Assembly of [September 12, 1893, the Dominion Government passed an Order in ' Council refusing the request. This Order, under date of June 30, 1894, says:
When the subject of rewards for services during the rebellion was under the consideration of the Government, a distinction was made between the Mounted Police, whose ordinary duties of maintaining law and order were within the limits of the disturbed districts, and the militia, who were called upon to leave their homes and occupations, at great personal inconvenience, resulting in many cases, in serious embarrassment to themselves and families. This distinction was marked by excluding the police from participation in the issue of scrip and by limiting the issue of the medal to those members of the Northwest [Mounted Police Force who were actually under Are.
For these reasons the scrip and medals to those not under fire were not granted. That was the successor to the Government of Sir John Macdonald. So the matter was before not only the Government of Sir John Macdonald, but before the Conservative Government of his immediate successor. Then the matter came before the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was also the head of the administration of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and on the 20th of August, 1900, an Order in Council was passed recommending that " The Northwest Mounted Police who were on service in the Northwest Territories during the period of rebellion of 1885 should he dealt with as far as regards the medal, in the same manner as members of'the active 
militia. ' So that the Order in Council of 10th July, 1886, was amended by striking out the words "who were actually under fire during the said troubles." In other words, the Mounted Police who were not under fire got the medal, but the law was not changed with reference to the grant of scrip, the Government adhering to the decision already reached by two preceding Governments.
The request was subsequently renewed to the Government which preceded the present one, and the same conclusion was reached. Therefore, when the matter came before the present Government, in view of the decision which had been reached by each successive Government during the period from 1886 down to date, the present Government thought it was not justified in opening up this olcf matter and changing the basis upon which this scrip was granted.
With reference to the Veterans Association to which my hon. friend has referred, I have nothing but the highest appreciation of that force and the branches of it at Vancouver and Victoria. I think it is only right to say that these men have offered to serve as a reserve force. They have made a very fine offer to the Government, and in the Bill which I hope to introduce into the House this week, because certain amendments to the law are rendered necessary by the changes which are being made,
I intend asking the House to approve of a provision in the law whereby a reserve of the Northwest Mounted Police may be created and these men who have served their country with such distinction as members of the^ force in the past constitute a reserve which may be called upon in emergency.
The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has brought out one fact to-night which had not come to my knowledge before, and that was that members of the permanent force in Canada did receive some recognition in the way of scrip. That matter I shall be glad to look into and see if it affects the situation as it comes before the Government.
My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. White) mentioned the question of the pay of the Mounted Police. Since the force came under my administration, two or three important changes have been made with reference to pay. First the pay has been increased fifty cents a day. Separation allowance is provided for the wives of all married men, and will continue to be provided until the general demobilization of the militia force is complete. An additional ration has

also been granted to each married man, so that all these combined constitute a substantial addition to the pay. I believe there is good ground for considering that probably some further advance should be made in the pay, and in the Bill which I expect to introduce I purpose recommending to the House that power be given to make a further increase in the pay of the mounted police. Members of the House will also bear in mind that in addition to the pay, pensions are provided for service in the force; and that has to be taken into consideration in considering the pay. As the law stands at present, a man who serves twenty years becomes entitled to a pension upon retirement. In the amendment which I contemplate bringing in, I purpose recommending to the House that the pension also be substantially increased. When these provisions are before the House I think that the hon. member for Victoria will feel that we are dealing absolutely fairly with the members of the force.
With reference to members of the force serving in the Arctic regions, I may say that a special allowance is made to them. They get a larger allowance than men serving in the better settled portions of the country, due no doubt to the higher cost of living in those higher latitudes. The hon. member for Victoria also asked why the force was not now as widely distributed as it was before. The chief reason is this: The provincial authorities, of course, are now responsible for the ordinary administration of law and order throughout the province, and it is not. necessary, having regard to the present duties of the force, that they should, be located in every town and village throughout 'the country.

I asked why they were centred in the large cities, because a great deal of their service is performed at some distance from headquarters. A man may have to go down the line a hundred miles from Edmonton, for instance, and then have to hire a car to take him to where he is required. If a detachment was located at Vermilion or Lloydminster, we will say, the men could go out from there at less expense, and it would be much cheaper for the married men to live and bring up their families; I also think they might be able to perform better service.

When the force is recruited up to strength there will be more detachments than at present. At present the view that those responsible for the
administration of the force entertain is that there is some gain in having a reasonably strong body of police at certain important points throughout the country. As regards the point raised by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) I shall not enter into a discussion of the cost of living. I appreciate what he says about the fine service which the force is rendering and the appreciation of the people of Northwestern Ontario of the fact that there is a force stationed there. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) and my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) both spoke on the question of increasing the force beyond the present strength. We are recruiting the force up to the present authorized strength, namely 1,200.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I\s it 1,200 yet?

It is not yet up to 1,200. My hon. friend from Port Arthur spoke about our asking the men who had been in the force and had gone overseas serving in Imperial units to come back into the force. That is part of the policy of the Government, and we have taken steps to bring to the attention of former members of the force who are now serving in Imperial units the fact that we shall be glad to welcome them back into the force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do these men know of these new regulations?

Some of them are only covered by the new Bill which is to be brought into the House, but the (substance of the regulations was posted up in France. We endeavoured as well as we could to Teach the men in the Imperial units, but it is not an easy matter to get into touch with men so widely scattered in so large a force. However, we have provided that any man who retired from the force in order to serve overseas in either the Canadian or the Imperial forces shall have his time service overseas counted in computing his pension, so that they will all have the benefit of the increased pension which we are providing and also the benefit, in computing the time for the pension, of the service they have rendered overseas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Has the Government considered extending the war service gratuity to the members of the Mounted Police who served in the Imperial forces?

That is a much larger
question, because there are not only the members of the Mounted Police who served in the Imperial forces but thousands of other men who went overseas to serve in
2.330

the Imperial forces. I do not see how it is possible to grant a supplementary war gratuity to men who left one branch of our service to serve overseas in the Imperial forces, and not treat every other British reservist in the same way. That is a question of policy which will have to be considered in relation to other departments of the Government as well as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. I said that we were recruiting up to the present strength. Possibly we should recruit beyond that strength, but that is a question that will have to receive very careful consideration and is now under the consideration of the .Government. If we decide to recruit beyond 1,200 it will be necessary for me to come to the House with a Supplementary Estimate to cover it. The present Estimates only cover recruiting up to 1,200.

How many commissions have been granted? In increasing tlie force there must be a great many officers, and I would like to know whether non-commissioned officers and others in the ranks are receiving any special consideration. Are the Government granting commissions to men in the lower ranks, or are they going outside of the force for their officers?
. Mr. ROWELL: Every commission so far granted has been a promotion from the ranks.

In support of the
remarks made by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) pointing out that permanent corps like A and B batteries received their scrip, I may say further that not only did the regular batteries receive it but a great many of the settlers that came into police headquarters or barracks as refugees with their families were sworn in to do guard duty. All these home guards really came in for protection but they were sworn to do duty while the police were out on patrol, and they were granted scrip as well as the others. I hope the minister has heard what I have said about that.

Yes, ll will note it.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
When this matter was
under consideration last, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) asked some questions in reference to increase of salary of $1,000 to the Deputy Minister. I do not see the hon. member in his place now. It will be borne in mind that the same increase has been granted to the Deputy Minister of Public Works as to all other Deputy Ministers in the public service. I can give no further explanation, because there is none to give. It has been decided as a matter of policy that all deputy ministers shall receive a salary of $6,000 a year, There are only two other items in regard to which inquiry was made. I was asked what had been the reduction in the inside service of the Public Works Department since I assumed the duties of office. There were actually in the department in October, 1917, 307 officials; in April 1919, there were 277 officials, or a reduction of 30. I was also asked how much of the total vote had not been expended last year because the positions were not all filled. The amount voted was $574,955, and we expended $503,130, leaving $71,825 unexpended. I imagine that in the appropriation I am asking for to-night there will be more than that amount which will not be expended. As some salaries may go up, I have decided to ask for an appropriation such as this but I want to assure the Committee that in future, as in the past, there will be no increase in the staff unless it is absolutely necessary. As fast as people leave the service by death or marriage, or whatever the cause may be, there will be no appointment to fill these positions unless they are actually necessary. I think, therefore, that there would be a larger balance unexpended at the end of the present fiscal year than there was at the end of last year.

The minister made a saving last year of $70,000 and he still asks for about the same sum this year. Why not reduce the Estimates proportionately if he expects to employ fewer rather than more? Does he expect to have a surplus next year?
I certainly think we will not expend the amount asked for in the appropriation.
You had a surplus last year of $70,000. Your Estimates should be reduced by that amount.

I am rather inclined to agree with my hon. friend, but in making up these Estimates in the department there is a strong feeling that we must provide for all contingencies, although I confess it does not look like good business.
Who is the chief architect of the Public Works Department?
Mr. Wright,
What has become of our good old friend, the late chief architect, Mr. Ewart?

Mr. Ewart is still in the department. He occupies a very responsible position as a sort of consulting architect in connection with the construction of the Parliament buildings. I want to say in the most public manner possible that I look upon him as perhaps one of the most valuable men we have in connection with the construction of that new building. While he is considerably over eighty years of age, he possesses all his faculties, he is at his office early and late and very many times in every month I call upon Mr. Ewart for information and he is always ready with it.
I see that there is an appropriation of $44,000, an increase of $14,000, for travelling expenses. It looks as if there is going to be more travelling, or more joy riding.

In my judgment no
money can be expended by any department, especially the department of Public Works, more profitably than that which is properly expended for travelling expenses. I have found occasion, several times during the past year, to send men from Halifax to Vancouver. We have expended on the construction of military hospitals and other military buildings, since the first of April in the last fiscal year
10 p.m. nearly $10,000,000. ^ There is hardly a day when a report does not come in from one of these stations, and we have found that we get the best results by sending a man from Ottawa to make a personal examination, come back and not only make a report but sit down and talk it over. I am personally asking for that increase. I will defend it as vigorously as may be necessary and I look upon it as the best way in which we can spend public money in order to get results.
