I am anxiously awaiting the day when we will be able to occupy a different chamber from this. Those who have to occupy the side benches are suffering a great disadvantage not only because of the difficulty of intelligently following the debates in this chamber, due to the acoustic properties, but also because of the crowded and irregular manner of the seating. It seems to me a lamentable condition of affairs that the Dominion Parliament should be constrained to discharge the greatest public duties that fall to any body under such extreme difficulties. I had hoped that last year would see the last of these conditions. I would like some assurance from the Minister of Public Works that every effort will be made to expedite the work and that the conditions will be represented to those responsible so that we can have some promise that next year we will be relieved from difficulties which, I feel certain, are very trying to a great many, especially the newer, members of the House.

I appreciate the difficulties that the minister has been operating under during the past year. I am sure that the situation has been very trying. I understand that there was an inspection of the new buildings made by some officials and members at an earlier period of the session. Most of us are not familiar with the present condition of the building, but I think it would be very interesting to the members if the minister would give to those who have not had an opportunity of making an inspection a statement as to how far the building is advanced, and what the possibility is of being in the new House next session.

I shall be very glad indeed to do so, because if there is one work in connection with the department that I have taken a personal interest in for the last year and a half it is the construction of the Parliament Building. I happen to be chairman of the parliamentary committee because of the position that I occupy. While I do not want to say anything that may be construed as reflecting upon any person, I

do not think I would be doing justice to m self, let alone to the House of Commons, if I did not say that I have been very much disappointed with the progress of the work. There has been nothing in my experience as a minister that has given me greater disappointment, I think, than the manner in which that work has been carried on. I have made myself almost a nuisance to many people in connection with it, but I have done my best anyway. I have told the workmen, and I propose to say here, that I do not think we have received value for the money we have paid out, and the fault is not all with the workmen either. There seems to be a general feeling on the part of pretty nearly every one connected with the institution that it is good, easy, government money, and that it is a great mistake to get through with the job too soon. For that reason I am having a lot of difficulty.
As to the possibilities of the future, I am not as pessimistic perhaps as one might gather from the statement I am making, because I do believe that, barring strikes, the building will be in such shape by the first of January next-and I presume there will not be a session of Parliament before that date,-that it can be occupied for parliamentary purposes.
But I may as well tell the Committee that the building will be in no way nearly completed. I believe the House of Cbmmons Chamber will certainly be ready for occupation, and probably pretty will advanced toward completion. The walls are practically all up; I mean the inside lining of stone is practically up. The ceiling is now being plastered and being got ready for the decorative work, and the galleries are started. Nothing has been done to the floors, but it seems to me that in the course of the next three or four months the House of Commons Chamber ought to be pretty well under way. I see no prospect of the Senate Chamber being ready for occupation unless there is a very great change in the movements of the men who are putting up the building.
Mr. THOMAS FOSTER; That will not affect the Commoners.

I think I should say
there are a number of very fine committee rooms in the building. There are very large reading rooms, and there are rooms which could be easily fitted up for the reception of the Senate for one session. The Senators would be much more comfortable than they are at the present time, and they would be

just as favourably situated as they were in the old House. The corridors will be pretty wTell finished, but probably not altogether. The building is different in the matter of entrances from the old structure; there are really three entrances instead of one. Members will recollect that in the old building everybody went in by the centre entrance and turned to the right and to the left. In the new building there will be a central entrance, which has not been started at all as far as finishing up is concerned, and I am sure, will not be completed. On the other hand there will be a lobby for the House of Commons, and one for the Senate. The House of Commons lobby is pretty nearly completed, in fact most of the floors are laid and the stonework in the walls is all completed. Workmen are now engaged upon the decorative work, but that portion of the building is practically completed now. The lobby on the Senate side has not been touched at all, so that it seems to me there is not much hopes of that being finished in time.
But there is another phase of the work which is much more encouraging than that upon which I have been dwelling. The rooms are in a very forward state of completion, and there will be, I think, about twice as much accommodation in the new building as there was in the old. The building is one story higher than the old structure, and it is laid off in a different way altogether. The Senate and House of Commons chambers were in the middle of the building before. Now the chambers are at the extreme ends, so that they have lots of sunlight and fresh air. The space that was occupied by the former Senate and Commons chambers is now taken up by what they call the office blocks, that is, two blocks extending for three floors after you go up the two floors. In other words, two floors are taken up in the elevation of the House of Commons and the Senate chambers and large committee rooms below, and there are three floors in each of these office blocks. I think there are eighty-four very fine rooms which are now practically completed, and when we get delivery of the marble those rooms will be ready for the painters and even for the installation of the furniture in a very short time. In addition to that, there are a tremendous number of rooms-I wrould not like to say the actual number, but it must go into hundreds-all around the building both front and rear. These rooms are now, I would say. three-fourths and perhaps four-

fifths plastered. The floors are laid, and in some cases, quite a number of cases, the plumbing is in a very advanced stage. The heating is also practically complete, so that there will be no question whatever of ample room for the accommodation of members, both of the Senate and House of Commons. With this condition of affairs, with the corridors in such a state that they will be passable, with the House of Commons chamber practically completed, and with plenty of room for the Senate, I see no reason in the world why we should not get into the building for the next session of Parliament.
I think I should state to the Committee, however, that the building is going to cost us a great deal more money than anybody ever imagined it would in the beginning. We have expended already a little over $5,000,000. I estimate that we will expend $2,000,000 during the coming year, and then it will not be anyway nearly complete. I have no accurate estimate with me to-night -I am sorry for that, because I might have had it-but I have not much hesitation in saying that the building will cost $8,000,000 when it is completed.
What was the original estimate of the cost?

About $5,000,000, possibly a little more. But we must remember that there has been an absolute revolution in the building trade since this structure was started/ Wages are very much in excess of what they were, as hon. gentlemen know; the cost of materials has gone up tremendously; and had we known everything, or had even my predecessors known everything-because the cost of things had gone up pretty well before I came into office- a saving might have been effected; but they did not like to buy too far ahead, there was always the hope that the war would be over and that there would be a reduction in the price of materials. Well, the war, unfortunately, lasted longer than people thought, the price of materials has not gone down, and therefore the building has cost a great deal more than was anticipated, due entirely to conditions over which perhaps no person had control.
Are you still paying eight per cent to the contractor?

No, the contract provides for the payment of eight per cent to the contractors up to $4,000,000, seven per cent for the next million, and nothing above $5,000,000, so that the percentage payable to. the contractors is practically earned. There is also a commission of five and a
half per cent which goes to the architect, and that also stops at $5,000,000.
Five and a half per cent on $5,000,000?
Five and a half per cent on an amount not exceeding $5,000,000.
Is that commission to the architects?
Yes.
What architects?
Well, Mr. Pearson, for one.
Is he not an employee of the Government under salary?

No, he gets a commission. The other architect is Mr. Marchand, of Montreal. I do not know just how the commission is divided, but Mr. Pearson gets by far the major portion of it. Mr. Pearson gets, I think, four-fifths, and Mr. Marchand the other one-fifth.

I was walking around
the library to-day, and I noticed a little shack behind it marked with a couple of red crosses and the inscription "hospital." I understand that at one time a doctor, or two doctors, were employed.
I think that is correct.
Are there two doctors still employed, or any medical man at all?
No, I am happy to say there are no doctors on the job, and there have not been for over a year.
Have there been any casualties on the works since the doctors left?
I have not heard of any.

That is the reason for dismissing the doctors then, I presume there were casualties before? When you got rid of the doctors there were not any casualties; the men did not fall down and get hurt. Who constitutes the committee that is supervising the construction at the present time?

I think I can give their names from memory. From the House of Commons there are, the Minister of Public Works, who is chairman; the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Marine. I think that is all. From the Senate there are, Senators Lougheed, Watson, and Robertson.
Was that Committee named by the late leader of the Opposition?
Senator Watson was so named.

Yes; and Dr. Pugsley, Mr. Lemieux and Mr. Murphy in the beginning. Mr. Murphy, I believe, never acted, and Mr. Lemieux resigned from the Committee at the time it was decided to tear down the old building and rebuild entirely. I believe that Sir Wilfrid Laurier refused to recommend appointments to the Committee after the retirement of Messrs. Murphy and Lemieux. After the Union Government was formed Dr. Pugsley retired, and Mr. Hazen also, and other gentlemen were appointed to fill the vacancies. Senator Watson, the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), and Senator Lougheed, I believe, are the only original members of the Committee.	[DOT]
Who supervised the purchase of materials?

That would be a pretty hard question to answer. For the last year and a half practically everything that could be purchased by public tender has been so purchased. A large part of the work that originally was intended to be carried out by the contractors has been done by a sort of subcontract-for instance, the heating. Members, if they have ever gone over the work, will perhaps realize that the building is to be heated from a central heating plant on the bank of the Ottawa river about a third of a mile from the buildings. The heat is conveyed by steam pipes through a tunnel which is all completed, the steam heats the water, and the hot water is pumped through the building. That work was all done by contract; that is, we called for tenders, a number of people tendered, and the work was given to the lowest tenderer, and he has completed his work.
Do the contractors get a commission on that?
Yes, 8 per cent; that is up to $5,000,000. The same is true of the plumbing.
Does that commission cease at 15,000,000?

Yes, the commission ceases when the cost reaches $5,000,000, and as the building has now cost $5,000,000, it really does not make very much difference because they will get no commission in the future. The same is true of the windows,

the doors and the woodwork; we called for tenders. There was a good deal of criticism of our standing by that principle in the case of the woodwork, because that was held to be artistic work which some person should be appointed to design and execute. However, we took the -ground that it was not impossible to draw specifications, and we did draw specifications and called for tenders. We gave one portion of the work to the lowest tenderer. As to the remainder, the next lowest tenderer withdrew his tender and the work went to the next lowest. We have followed that principle wherever possible, and we have found it possible in nearly every instance. I can scarcely recall the purchase of anything since I have been on the committee that has not been by tender; in fact, any exception would be a matter of very, very minor importance. Of course, we are reaching the point -where some of the work cannot be done by tender. We have just completed arrangements with a gentleman to come here and design centres, ceilings, and decorations of that kind. Tenders cannot be called for for that particular work; it has to be done by hiring some person of artistic leanings to carry it out. The same will be true of many other things in the future. But I can assure the Committee that wherever it has been possible we have called for tenders, and invariably the contract has gone to the lowest tenderer, except, I think, one case, the details of which I have forgotten, but there were very good reasons there for departing from our rule.
Has the architect been paid the full amount of his commission?
I am not positive about that. I think there is some little question at issue.
Does he get 5 per cent on the total cost?
He gets 5i per cent.

The reason I ask that question is that the architect is getting a very large sum of money and there are particular points about his work that will not be known until the building is completed,-such, for example, as the acoustics. If he has made a mess of that he should not be paid the full amount of his commission, because that is a matter

of vital importance. It has been discussed frequently in the House, and the attention of the present minister and of the former minister has been drawn to it. If we get a chamber like this, for example, where we cannot hear what is being said, it would be a calamity after spending so much money, and the architect is the man to take responsibility for that. Then there is the ventilation, which was very bad in the old Chamber, and which we all hope will be good in the new one. I was disappointed to see a corridor around the lower part of the building so that the Chamber is not exposed to the fresh air on any side as this Chamber is; the upper part is. But the acoustics is a matter of vital importance, and if the architect has not been paid his full commission, I would suggest that a portion be retained until the building is completed and it is known if he has done his work properly or not.

I appreciate the point made by my hon. friend. Of course, I am not responsible for the contract. I have watched the construction of the new building pretty carefully from the standpoint of the architect. I do not think my hon. friend need have the least fear that it will not be the best that money can build-at least, I have seen no evidence of any attempt to stop the expenditure of money. There is one thing sure from Mr. Pearson's standpoint-and I want to say it to his credit, because it is a great national structure,- that he is determined that it shall be the very best of its kind that can be produced. I have discussed with him a good many times the question of acoustics. He has gone to different places in the States to investigate-in fact, he wants to go to Great Britain, and I rather advise that he should be allowed to go in order to discuss and investigate this very important question, because we all realize that the acoustics of the Chamber is the most important in connection with the whole enterprise, outside of having a substantial building. As to the ventilation, if my hon. friend would just take a forenoon and go through the building he would satisfy himself beyond question that the ventilation has been looked after in a manner that has never been attempted before.
How do you get through the fence?

I think if my hon. friend will present his card he will find no difficulty in getting through-in fact,
they will be only too happy to send some one with him to point out the different features of construotion. Those are the instructions, and I am sure they will be carried out. In fact, I have asked and suggested that members take the trouble to go through the buildings, and I think they ought to do so. If my hon. friend would go into the building and go down into the' basement, he would find miles of galvanized iron pipes, some of them four and five feet in diameter, extending all through the building. They come up into the chamber out of the wall about six feet from the floor, and fresh air is being constantly pumped from pipes outside of the building through the basement up through those pipes and distributed throughout the chamber. Then there are other pipes, such as we have in this building, ventilating pipes that take the old air away. I cannot give my hon. friend any guarantee as to the acoustics, but I can absolutely assure him that there will be no question about the ventilation. That takes place in all portions of the building where it is neceskary to have ventilation. I do not think that takes place in what they would call the ordinary members' rooms, although it does to some extent. All the windows in the members' rooms are casement windows. There is no wood about them whatever; they are made of steel, copper and glass with a small lever by which they are opened and thrown out a little way, and a thumb-screw keeps them at any angle at which the member wants them.
Is there a clerk of works in charge of the construction of the building? That is usual in large buildings of this kind. If so, is he paid by the contractor or by the Government?
In justice to Mr. Pearson, I should have stated-and I intended to when I had the opportunity-that Mr. Pearson himself employs all of his own staff out of the 51 per cent.
That is the clerk of works who looks after the construction work?

Mr. Pearson is responsible for the inspection as the work proceeds. Hon. members must not run away	with	the idea that Mr. Pearson gets the whole four-fifths of 51 per cent and gives nothing for it. He has quite a large staff and his expenditures will be very considerable. We may regret the cost of this work, and I have.

perhaps, somewhat disagreed with Mr. Pearson, and sometimes, I think, the work has not been done too well in some portions, but that does not make any difference, it is being done the very best it ds possible to do it under the circumstances. Mr. Pearson has a competent staff and is responsible for seeing that the work is properly carried out.

* The minister said he was very much dissatisfied with the progress of the work, but he did not tell us just how or why. The question arises as to the commissions to be paid to both the contractor and the architect. If the building up to this time has cost approximately $5,000,000, or the amount that the commission is to be paid on to the architect, what arrangement has been made for the completion of the building? The architect is paying out probably several thousand dollars a month in carrying out his portion of the work. Will he continue until this work is completed to pay that money out of his own pocket, or will an arrangement be made to pay him out of the public treasury? The same thing may be said with regard to the contractor. If his commission ends at a cost of $5,000,000, and the building is estimated to cost $8,000,000 and will go on for another year before it is completed, what provision has been made for supervision by the contractor and the architect?

There is no provision
whatever. They receive this commission on $5,000,000. Of course, the money has not all been paid to them; there is a certain drawback still coming to them.
About how much?

The note I have says
that one-fifth of the commission which is to be paid upon the whole $5,000,000, will be paid upon the completiop of the preliminary sketches. The remaining four-fifths is [DOT]to be paid pro rata from time to time as payments are made to the contractor. I know some money is being held back as regards Mr. Pearson. There is no provision made for that balance, but it must be remembered that these are honourable gentlemen and that they have received up to the present time a fair return for services rendered. I think I can state both as regards Mr. Lyall and Mr. Pearson that they will go on regardless of whether there will be any more commissions or not. I am satisfied that Mr. Pearson is so wrapped up in the work that if it took the rest of his natural life, he would gladly give it to stay there and see that the work was properly executed. Mr. Pearson, I think, looks upon
[Mr. Oarve'U.J
it as his life's work, and regardless of commissions in the future, Mr. Pearson will stay there and see the work through and make it just as great a success as he possibly can. In saying that as regards Mr. Pearson, I do not wish to cast any discredit upon Mr. Lyall, but Mr. Lyall does not look upon this in the same manner as Mr. Pearson does. Mr. Lyall has many other business interests in Canada and he has to look after them. Mr. Lyall has, unfortunately, been ill for the last three months, and has not been able to give this work any personal attention at all, but from a conversation I have had with him only last week, there is no question he will be able to give it his personal attention and his staff will be there, and this work will proceed just as well in the future as it has done in the past. [DOT]
What is the cause of the delay?

I can put it in very plain language. There is a feeling when men are working for the Government that it is good, easy money and there is no good hurrying themselves too much. It is just that tem-peramentality running through the whole thing. I have told the workmen to their faces what I am saying here, namely, that I do not think they have given us value for our money. Sometimes they disagree with me and sometimes they blame somebody besides themselves, but that is my view of the matter. And the last time I met them, which was one day only last week, I certainly told them in plain language what I thought about the matter and what I hoped would be the case in the future.

The minister stated that the heating plant was stationed one-third of a mile away from the .building. Any person who understands the conveying of heat from a unit to a building must realize that there is a very large percentage of waste. Why was that heating plant put so. far away from the building?

I cannot give the reason why. I have seen nothing to lead me to believe that it is not one of the most up-to-date heating plants in the world to-day. There is this about it: The pipes go through a concrete subway six feet by seven, and if the subway does not stand it is not because enough steel and concrete were not put into it, because reinforced steel was put in underneath even over bed-rock, so that it is going to stay there. There will be no chance for cold getting in; there will be no condensation, and the subway, fortunately, is

all uphill from the time the steam leaves the plant until it gets into the building.
I am told that the amount of condensation or loss will be extremely small. The pipes, I think, are nine or ten inches in diameter. The east and west blocks, the Langevin block and the Supreme Court buildings are all to be heated from the same central .plant. The engineers have figured out that there will be a very substantial saving in the heating of these buildings from a central plant, as compared with individual plants for the several buildings. But this is an engineering matter, and I have not expert knowledge on the subject. I would gay, however, that the engineers must be right, and personally I look for no trouble whatever.
How far below the surface is the main conduit to the building?

On an average it is from three to four feet below the surface of the street to the top of the tunnel; the tunnel is seven feet deep and six feet wdde. These pipes are suspended in the tunnel, and there are manholes at a few places so that repairs can be made, but these "are all air tight. The pipes will be protected by asbestos, and every precaution will be taken that there shall be as little loss as possible in transmission. There is this further advantage: there will be no furnaces, and consequently no soot or dust around the building. This plan, I think, will effect a great economy and be of great advantage from the sanitary standpoint.
, Mr. L. A. LAPOINTE:	Does the minister's estimate of $8,000,000 include the cost of the furniture?

No, I do not think so. I hope that the committee will realize that when I said $8,000,000, that is only an approximate estimate. My reason for saying that is this:	I know about what is expected to be done during the coming year, and I know that $2,000,000 will not finish the tower; in fact, it will not do much more than lay the foundation for the tower. I think it will take $8,000,000 to finish the building exclusive of furniture. We have not considered the question of furniture yet, and I must confess I am somewhat at a loss to know how to go about it.

Are you going to use mahogany?
!M>r. CARVELL:	I presume there will
be certain rooms that should be finished in mahogany. I do not see how tenders
can be called for for furniture, because you cannot very well draw up specifications. A number of the biggest firms have been discussing the matter and would like to have a chance to tender. I can only say that they will all have the opportunity, but I think even before that time comes, some artistic brain must be set to work to advise the colour schenje and the general arrangement of the furniture and rugs and things of that kind. I confess that it is beyond me. I think I know something about the building, but I am not an expert on the artistic side of it. I can assure the Committee, however, that nothing will be done in the matter until it has been thoroughly considered.

The statement of the minister to-night is very encouraging, so fai as it holds out a reasonable prospect of the House occupying the new building next session. It will be a great relief to us who have spent several sessions in this building to get into the new building with all its conveniences and comforts. I should like to impress upon the Committee that the architect and the contractors are not the only ones who have a personal interest in the building. Every member of the House has a very direct personal interest in it, and while many of us may not occupy a seat in it for a great number of years, our successors will. The members of the House of Commons and of the Senate who are privileged to occupy seats in this and future Parliaments will be compelled to spend a very large portion of their lives in that building, and I think men who have spent from twelve to fifteen hours a day for five or six months of each year in this building are entitled to the very greatest degree of comfort that it is possible to give them in the new building now being erected. I trust that the inner arrangements for the comfort of the members will not be overlooked in the larger plan of producing a fine building. I have had the privilege of going over the building two or three times, the last time only a few weeks ago, and from what an inexperienced person like myself could see I must say that the building promises a very great degree of comfort indeed for the individual members of the House. That is necessary if we are to give our best to Parliament. The conditions here prevent us giving our best work; they are destructive to the interest that we take in the House, for the simple reason that we are unable to follow its proceedings. I would therefore again



impress upon the Committee the necessity of seeing that the very greatest possible degree of comfort and convenience is provided for the individual members of the House and Senate.

I quite appreciate the necessity of everything my hon. friend has indicated, and I can assure him that everything is being done that can reasonably be done in order to meet the requirements he has mentioned. There will be sufficient rooms m the new building to give every man who wishes it a private office. I do not imagine that every man will wish it, because in some cases two members would prefer to be together, but I think I can safely say that there will be sufficient space to give every man who really wishes it a private office. The offices will be suitably furnished. The floors will be of nailacrete, which is a little softer than concrete. Over that will be a covering of battleship linoleum, and over that a carpet or rug of some kind. Suitable desks, chairs, lounges and things of that kind will be provided. There will be a hot and cold water basin in every room, I believe, and ten elevators in the building. Lavatories will be provided where required. In my judgment one of the greatest comforts and conveniences of the whole building will be the restaurant, which is being built above the Commons Chamber. Not only will it be beautiful in design, but, overlooking the Ottawa river, I think it has one of the prettiest locations I have ever seen in my life. The kitchens will be on a very elaborate scale. Hon. members can rest assured that everything will be done to provide for their comfort and health and for that of the officials of the House and all those who have to live within its precincts.
Will accommodation be provided in the building, for the Speaker of the Commons and the Speaker of the Senate?
It has been decided that the Speakers of the respective Houses shall not reside in the building.

I appreciate the last remarks of the minister in regard to the arrangement of the new Parliament buildings and am pleased to see that some interest is being taken in the comfort and personal satisfaction of private members. My experience of the old Parliament was very short, but I found when I came there that I occupied a room in the cellar with five or six other members. We had some sort of desks but there was not a bookcase of any kind in which one could keep books or papers, and 	-	'
we did not find it very convenient. We did not expect anything elaborate here, but it would be impos|sible for members to do any kind of decent work in the rooms we are occupying here, there being as many as eight or ten in some rooms, and not fewer than four or five in any. It makes it very inconvenient and practically impossible for members to prepare their work. I am not very fastidious about the furniture that is in the rooms. In my room now I have an old desk that was brought down in pieces from the -fire in the old Parliament building and nailed together. However, I have not made any requisition for furniture. I may, but I do not-know that the Minister of Public Works would grant my request if I did. Speaking seriously, I am very glad to hear the minister tell us that in the new Parliament buildings there will be proper facilities and plenty of room. One or two in a room is all right, but in order to carry on the work of the session and to do any other work which may be necessary, proper facilities are indispensable. We regret that we have had to remain here so long, and trust this will be the last session. It would be gratifying for those who will have the privilege of being in the new building to have adequate convenience and comfort.
Will there be provided a recreation room in the shape of a gymnasium for the use of members? I am quite serious about this.

I am serious too, and I will go so far as to say that it has been considered, although I do not think it has been done. I may State what Mr. Pearson has suggested to me, and what I would regard with favour. He proposes that there be a walk all round the library, a place that can be kept in the winter time at a fairly warm temperature, where members can exercise. The suggestion appeals strongly to me.	As to a real gymnasium or anything of that kind, I do not think that has been considered, although if it were thought necessary 11 think space enough could be found in the basement to provide almost anything like that, because there are two floors below the ground floor. There is much more space there than one would ever think unless he went through the building, so that if it were thought advisable to adopt this proposal there could be no difficulty about it.

I am very glad that the hon. member drew attention to that feature

of the building. There has been a commendable unanimity of opinion amongst members that the new building should conduce to the comfort of the members both of the House of Commons and of the Senate. We spend long hours here, especially the members of the House of Commons. No eight-hour a day schedule applies to members of the House of Commons, and even the shortest day is a long day, and would be considered by any person in any other walk of life as requiring " time and a half " at least if not " double pay " for overtime. We are here twelve, fifteen and sixteen hours a day, week after week a nd month after month, and I say in all seriousness that there should be some provision whereby members who have an hour or an hour and a half at their disposal can take systematic exercise. That is a' common-sense view of the matter. Personally it has always been a case of putting off exercise from day to day, but if there were a gymnasium room-and there would be ample space for a place of that kind-the members could take half an hour and go for an exercise with benefit to their health. Since the minister says that this matter has come up for consideration, I would suggest the advisability of appointing a .Committee of this House-I do not know that it would be necessary to have a Committee of the Senate, although we might have some of the younger members of that body if it were thought fit-to confer with the Committee who have supervision of this work to consider the question of having some recreation room in the new building. Some may regard this as of little consequence, but in my opinion it is a matter of great importance, and I would like the question to be seriously considered.
Mr. -OARVELL: I do not by any means consider it a matter of small consequence. On the contrary, I have been discussing it with the architects for the last year, and while we have not agreed upon what shall be done it has been practically decided that there shall be a promenade indoors, to which members can resort in winter time. I would very heartily welcome the advice and assistance of a committee of the House. I will bring the matter up at the next meeting of the Parliamentary Committee and also take rneans, if the House deems fit, to see that a committee is appointed to discuss the question with the Parliamentary Committee, because it is something that touches the health of every member. I do not suppose there are half a dozen members who
149i
do not realize that they are not getting sufficient exercise. I am not getting the? exercise I should, largely because there is. no opportunity without going off to the Yj M.C.A. I regard the matter as of great importance and will take whatever steps are necessary to see that it is brought up in the way suggested.

As a medical man, I
strongly support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and endorsed by the Minister of Public Works, because I think it is very essential that men who are doing mental work, as we are here, should get sufficient exercise. We are all getting on toward middle life-I would not say that anyone of us was getting past that stage,-and we should consider seriously the establishment of a few rooms in the basement for a (gymnasium and place of exercise, where there might also be a few shower baths. This would be all that would be necessary and it would be practically inexpensive. Tt would give a fair amount of exercise to most members, and the members of the Press Gallery could also work off some of their superfluous energy there.
Do I understand the, hon. minister to say that practically the whole of the commission to the architects; has been paid out?
It has been all earned and a substantial amount paid out.

It is of course gratifying to know that we are dealing with honourable gentlemen who will fulfil their; obligations. But even when one is dealing, with honourable gentlemen, regard must be* had to business principles. Do we understand that in the making of these contracts the arrangement is of such a nature that we may pay the architect the entire amount of his compensation while the building is little more than half completed?

I have not the contract before me but I am pretty sure that is about the substance of it. Of course, I can do nothing but carry out the contract. There is no actual written contract with the architects, but there is sufficient correspondence in existence to practically make up a contract. There was some little question whether the commission would be allowed on one certain item, and I believe that a formal contract had never been signed. The fact that -the building is going, to cost 12,250.000 or $3,000,000 more than anticipated does not make any difference at all; we take it for granted that the architects

are entitled to their commission on $5,000,000. I am not in a position to say how much has been paid- out, but I know that practically the whole amount has been paid, because the contract calls for it. They get their commission monthly upon the expenditure. That is the contract.

If that is the contract, of course the minister must fulfil it, but ordinary business principles would seem to indicate that the commission should be paid out pro rata with the progress of the building. Supposing anything should happen to these most excellent gentlemen, of whom I am quite sure I cannot speak too highly, suppose they should be called by death, you would have a building a little more than half completed, the commission paid out and nobody to supervise the work for the remainder of the time.
Were there two contracts, one with the contractors and one with the architects?	*
Yes.

Who are the architects
who appear in the contract?
Mr. 'CARVELL: Mr. Pearson and Mr. Marchand, of Montreal.
Are they in partnership?

In a way. Mr. Marchand acts in an advisory capacity and attends meetings of the committee whenever anything of importance is going on. Mr. Pearson acts as resident architect and inspector of the work and has personal charge.

If a contract has been entered into between these two architects, plans must have been prepared and submitted to the Department of Public Works here. If such was the case, I would like to know whether the plans were prepared by Mr. Pearson or Mr. Marchand and what commission the Government agreed to pay for the preparation of the plans. I understand that there would be a commission paid for the preparation of the plans and also a commission for the supervision of the work.

They were to be paid one-fifth of the commission upon the whole $5,000,000 upon the completion of the preliminary sketches. It always seemed to me that that payment was entirely out of proportion to the amount of work performed.
That is paid to them jointly?

Yes, it is a joint contract and they have a private arrangement between themselves as to the division. Then the balance of the amount is paid monthly according to the progress estimates. I feel pretty sure that the bulk of that amount has been paid out both to the architects and the contractors.
Is there provision in the contract by which, if the cost of the work should exceed $5,000,000, the commission shall be reduced?
No; they simply get 8 per cent up to $4,000,000 and 7 per cent on the next million, and nothing on any amount expended beyond that.
If il should require the minister to place on the Table a copy of the two contracts I hope he will be able to do so and that we will have an opportunity of seeing them.
I shall be delighted to get them.

The minister said that
the architects were paid monthly on progress estimates. Who makes these estimates?

They are made up by our own staff very largely. Mr. Ewart occupies the position of consulting architect for the department and all of this work is under his special care and attention. He has a staff with him. The deputy minister has to pass on everything, and he is in a sense a member of this parliamentary committee. All the progress estimates are supervised, revised and scrutinized in every way possible by the department before the estimates are paid. The architect makes the plans, and directs the contractor what he shall do and how he shall do it. We have men who are looking after the timekeeping and these reports are handed in to the Public Works Department. The department, under the supervision of Mr. Ewart, goes over these matters fortnightly and makes up the pay list. Outside of the pay list practically everything for the last year and a half has been a matter of contract. There is a pretty extensive pay list. We have something over 600 men employed directly under the contract of Mr. Lyall, and I do not know how many men there are who are carrying out these various subcontracts to which I referred a short time ago.

Has the minister in mind any plan whereby he might hasten this

work? Could the department take over the work themselves, get better results and get the work done more quickly? I do not know what the rate of pay to the men is, but as a general thing when men are getting satisfactory pay they work pretty well provided it is not made to look like a life job to them. We have this undertaking costing $5,000,000, which is practically a dead investment until the work is completed. If you could hasten the completion of the building you would save $250,000 or more a year on the investment. You might bonus the employees to get the work done quicker, and if you did so it would be a great convenience to the members and a benefit to the people generally.

I am afraid my hon. friend is a little late in his plea for the employees, because they have signed an agreement that will fix their wages until next year. If he had made his plea eight or nine days ago he might have got some political benefit, but that time has gone by now. These employees are getting pretty well paid and they have come to an agreement with the employers in Ottawa. I had nothing to do with it at all. The contractors employing help got together with the workmen, our workmen included, and came to an agreement that was satisfactory to the men and which was signed by them. This contract runs until the first of May, 1920. I do not think there is much use in talking about a bonus to the men. As to the contractors, I do not think anybody will seriously consider that I should pay them a bonus, because I think the sense of this committee is that they are fairly well paid as it is. We possibly might have taken the work out of the contractors' hands but I do not know that any good would have been accomplished by it, I think it would have been a great mistake to have taken it out of the Lyalls' hands.
They might be quite willing to be relieved of it now.

They might be quite willing to be relieved now. I do not feel like relieving them of it. When I came in I was bound by the contract. I do not feel like violating contracts unless there are strong reasons for doing so. But I can say frankly that I have not been satisfied with the progress of the work. I repeat it here. I am doing all I can anyway, but I shall endeavour to see that the work goes a little faster in the future than in the past.

I am not trying to make any political capital with regard to labour,
I represent a farming constituency, and I ain not at all worrying about that phase of the matter. But I have had some experience in the building business, and I made it a practice to give my men a bonus if they completed the work before a certain date. I always had good results with that system, and got the work completed much faster than other fellows around who were trying to keep wages down and would not resort to the bonus system. In this case the contrac-tors^are practically through as far as regards getting a bonus. Now, they may be honourable men, but as the minister pointed out, they are not spending very much time here,, because they have other work to look after, and if the Government could save money and get into the building sooner I do not believe there would be any great difficulty in cancelling the contract.	.
Does the hon. gentleman believe in that policy in regard to all Government buildings?

I now wish to take up an item in the Supplementary Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1919.
Ottawa Parliament Building-Restoration, $773,000.
Air. 'CARVELL: I think last year a million and a half was voted, but it did not take care of the work. The money was advanced, I think, out of the war funds temporarily, and we are now asking Parliament to vote this Supplementary Estimate to provide for the work that was not covered in the Estimates as passed by Parliament last year.
That is for the past year?

Yes. It is included in the estimate I have given of $5,000,000, as being the cost of the work up to the present time.'
Progress reported.
